subtopic: STATEMENT ON WELCOME TO HER MAJESTY IN CHICAGO

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON WELCOME TO HER MAJESTY IN CHICAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I would like to say a word or two with regard to the events yesterday in Chicago. That city and the state of Illinois accorded to Her Majesty the Queen and Prince Philip a welcome which was certainly unequalled in my experience. It was one that typifies the relationship between the commonwealth and the United States in which Canada has a particular interest.
The warmth of the reception and the scope of the welcome accorded Her Majesty and the prince was an unforgettable experience and enduring evidence, I believe, not only of the esteem in which the Queen is held but also of that regard, important as it is, which the people of the United States showed yesterday they have for the necessity for and the preservation of unity in freedom as between the United States and the commonwealth.
I want to say one word more, if I may, of thanks and appreciation to the mayor of the city of Chicago and the governor of the state of Illinois and those associated with them for the outstanding arrangements which were made in order to make yesterday a day of historic significance.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON WELCOME TO HER MAJESTY IN CHICAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I once had the privilege of living in Chicago in the days when Big Bill Thompson was the mayor of that great city, and when I suspect a visit from the King or the Queen of England might not have been received so enthusiastically as yesterday's visit was. It is encouraging to learn from the Prime Minister that all the vigour and vitality of that great city was directed to giving the Queen of Canada and Prince Philip such a warm welcome. I am sure it was appreciated by the Queen and the prince, and that they had good cause to realize that Chicago is not only warm in its
welcome, but also that it is a city of art galleries and symphony orchestras as well as stockyards.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON WELCOME TO HER MAJESTY IN CHICAGO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the members of the C.C.F. group are very pleased at the tremendous tribute given to the Queen and Prince Philip by the people of the city of Chicago. We agree with the Prime Minister that it was a tribute to the person who occupies the position of Queen of Canada and to Prince Philip. It was also a tribute to the very good relations between Canada and the United States, and to the esteem that we feel is held for Canadians and for Canada in the great and friendly nation to the south.

speechtext:
should like to make a statement with respect to the government's proposals regarding Bill No. C-59, about which inquiries have been made from time to time by the Leader of the Opposition and others.
Bill C-59 was designed to accomplish two main purposes; first, to clarify and improve the law relating to combinations, mergers and monopolies; and second, to enact three provisions for the protection of small business and consumers against unfair practices, including misleading advertising.
Since the introduction of the bill we have received representations from businessmen and trade associations that the measure should be deferred until they have had an opportunity to study it more thoroughly and make representations with respect to the combines and merger provisions. In a matter of this kind it is of particular importance that all interests have every reasonable opportunity to make their submissions.
We have therefore decided that the proper course is to proceed with those parts of the bill which relate to the problems of small business, because we believe them to be urgent and because there have not been the requests for opportunities for further representations in this connection that there have been in connection with the other matter; and to defer until next session the provisions relating to combinations, mergers and monopolies and the other incidental provisions of the bill. The provisions we propose to

Business of the House
proceed with, if the house agrees, are the enactment of the three provisions relating particularly to small business, including the section on misleading advertising. It will also be necessary to introduce a fourth provision dealing with the situation in the fishing industry in British Columbia.
A statement of evidence has been submitted by the director under the combines act to the restrictive trade practices commission and to various fish packing companies, associations and individuals, alleging that certain agreements and activities relating to the supply of raw fish by the fishermen to the companies are illegal. As a result of the doubt thereby cast upon the legality of such agreements and activities the companies have declined to negotiate prices with the fishermen's union, as they have done in past years, and it appears that a strike may result which could lead to the loss of the salmon catch and perhaps other catches of fish.
There is a provision in the anti-combines legislation to the effect that nothing therein shall be construed to apply to combinations of workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection as such workmen or employees, and it will, I believe, be argued by the fishermen that they come within the protection of this provision. If, however, it should turn out, as a result of the inquiry, that the agreements dealt with therein are in whole or in part illegal, it may be that the report will disclose a situation with which we shall have to take steps to deal in a definitive manner, but it is not possible to do so now.
Meanwhile it is essential that all reasonable steps be taken to prevent the loss of the salmon and other catches, and I shall therefore propose a clause in the new bill to the effect that the anti-combines legislation shall not apply to arrangements between fishermen or associations of fishermen in British Columbia, and persons or associations of persons engaged in the buying or processing of fish in British Columbia, relating to the prices, remuneration or other conditions under which fish shall be caught and supplied, between the 1st day of January, 1959 and December 31, 1960. By the latter date it is hoped that the remaining steps in the inquiry will have been concluded and a report will have been made by the restrictive trade practices commission so that we may be able to assess what, if any, further action should be taken to dispose finally of the situation.
I have spoken to the Leader of the Opposition and to the leader of the C.C.F. party about this matter, and in accordance with those discussions, and for the reasons I have

outlined, I would request the unanimous consent of the house to drop the order for second reading of Bill C-59 in order that I may introduce a new bill containing only the three provisions in the present bill which I have mentioned and the new provision regarding the fishing situation in British Columbia.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Kootenay West asked me a question relating to the establishment of an additional quarantine inspection point near Montreal being used jointly by Canadian and U.S. authorities. My department had felt this station was necessary to take care of all vessels bound for the seaway rather than at Montreal, and as a gesture of courtesy the U.S. staff were invited to occupy offices in the same building.
This offer was accepted, with agreement between my officers and those of the U.S. public health service that the anchorage off Longue Pointe would be used as a common inspection point for all vessels. Those vessels bound for United States ports after leaving the seaway would be examined and cleared by the United States staff, while those bound for Canadian ports would be cleared by Canadian staff. Thus all vessels would be assured of further passage through the seaway without delay for this purpose.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The only occasion when a Canadian citizen might receive an examination from a United States official would be if he happened to be a passenger or crew member of a vessel first calling at a U.S. port on leaving the seaway. In this case, of course, he would receive exactly the same treatment as though he were on a vessel proceeding direct to, say, the port of New York.
This practice of close co-operation between Canadian and United States quarantine staffs is an arrangement of long standing that has resulted in vastly increased convenience to all forms of cross-border traffic. It is similar to methods in the immigration and customs services-on cross-border trains, for example- and quite often entails operations of officers from locations in the neighbouring country rather than their own.

Those are a few points on which I thought I should comment. The need and desirability of crop insurance are indicated by the large number of representations which have been made. Representations for crop insurance have been made by provinces, farm organizations, and associations of rural municipalities. Nearly all of these called for crop insurance schemes involving federal-provincial cooperation.
66968-9-354J
Proposed Crop Insurance
Many members are familiar with the extreme variations in crop yields throughout the country and with the difficulties that crop failures impose on farmers, on communities and on the nation. Weather hazards including drought, excessive moisture, frost and hail have caused most of the damage. Other factors such as insects and disease have taken their toll. In looking at the yields of various crops across the country it is found that yields are frequently less than one haif of the long term average yield. Between 1921 and 1956 in Manitoba, seven of 14 crop districts have had wheat yields below 50 per cent of the average. One crop district had four such years. In Saskatchewan all crop districts have had wheat yields below 50 per cent of the average during this period, and one crop district had 10 such years. In Alberta 11 of the 16 crop districts have had wheat yields below 50 per cent of the long term average. One crop district had seven such years, another six and another five. The variation in oats and barley yields in the prairie provinces has been somewhat similar. In addition, many individual farmers have had crop failures when the average yield for the crop district has been high. Another indication of the frequency of crop failure in the prairie provinces is the number of awards made under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. More than one million awards to farmers have been made since the program was started in 1939.
In British Columbia, although yield records for such a long period were not available, there have also been crop failures. The main crops experiencing failure were apples, cherries and peaches. In eastern Canada the variations in crop yields are less than in the prairie provinces but farmers occasionally experienced failures in crops such as tobacco, soybeans, sugar beets, apples and potatoes.
Crop failures are disastrous to farmers and their families because they find it difficult, if not impossible, to maintain a reasonable level of living until they are able to harvest the next crop. Also, farmers are not able to carry on their farming operations in an efficient manner if they have not the means to do so. Crop failures are felt in the community because business activity declines. Crop failures have their effect on the nation, too, since the demand for farm equipment and supplies declines with the resultant effect upon employment, business and trade. It is therefore considered to be in the interests of the nation as well as in the interests of farmers that crop insurance schemes be implemented.
The present insurance facilities are limited. The main program which provides assistance in the event of crop failures is the Prairie
5586	HOUSE OF
Proposed Crop Insurance Farm Assistance Act. Under this program payments of up to $2 per acre-$4 on one-half of the cultivated acreage-are made to farmers in areas of crop failure. The maximum payment to a farmer is $800. About one half of the funds paid to farmers has been collected from farmers in the form of a 1 per cent levy on sales of grain. Although recent amendments have greatly improved the kind of assistance available under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, it does not meet the needs of a national and comprehensive [DOT]crop insurance program.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act was designed for the prairie provinces and primarily for grain production. Its provisions would not be applicable to other crops in other parts of the country. Also, the limited amount of assistance available under that scheme, the fact that it does not deal with individual cases of crop failure, and the fact that it has certain other inequities mean that it does not have the advantages of crop insurance schemes even in the prairie provinces.
The other main kind of insurance available to some farmers is hail insurance. Hail insurance is generally available in the prairie provinces and in some other parts of the country. Hail insurance, however, does not cover the crop losses experienced by farmers from many other causes.
There are several reasons why the present bill is a measure to assist provinces in operating crop insurance programs. Most representations have requested that the crop insurance scheme be one involving both the federal and provincial governments. Farmers in all provinces probably do not want crop insurance at this time. This act would permit each province to decide whether or not crop insurance would be offered to farmers in their own province. Provincial governments are in a better position to establish the kind of scheme which is best suited to the particular conditions existing in their own provinces. There is a wide variety of crops grown in the country, a wide variety of farming methods and differences of viewpoint as to the kind of insurance schemes which would be most effective. Provincial governments would be in a better position to assess these and to implement the kind of program best suited to those conditions.
Some people, some organizations, and perhaps some provinces consider that a crop insurance scheme has to be compulsory in order to be most effective. The federal government has not the authority to impose compulsory crop insurance schemes on farmers. For these reasons the bill provides for assistance to provinces which undertake to implement crop insurance programs.
[Mr. Harkness.l

The question of the amount and kind of assistance has received careful consideration. It is considered that some assistance is necessary in order to make a crop insurance program available to farmers. Up to the present time no assistance has been available and no provincial government nor any other agency has offered a comprehensive crop insurance program. In the United States assistance has been available to the extent of administration costs. After 20 years of operation only about 27 per cent of eligible wheat producers carry crop insurance. In order to encourage a more rapid participation, a greater amount of assistance than is offered under the United States program is proposed in this bill.
Mention might be made of the Unemployment Insurance Act which provides incomes to workers whose source of income has been cut off through circumstances beyond their control. It is in the interests of the workers, the community and the nation that workers have this income in periods when their ordinary source of income is cut off. The federal government makes a contribution to this program by way of paying administration costs and part of the premiums. Similarly in farming, when crops are lost through no fault of the farmer, and his income is lost, it is desirable to have some means of providing farmers with a source of income. As in the case of unemployment insurance it is considered appropriate that there should be federal contributions to the program. It is estimated that the contributions for crop insurance outlined in this bill would be about the same proportion of the total expenditure under the program as in the case of the unemployment insurance program.
This bill follows the principle adopted in the case of hospital insurance, where the federal government makes contributions to the cost of hospital services and leaves the administration of the program to the various provinces. The provinces are free to adapt the program to their own circumstances and desires. They are free to make financial contributions to the program or to charge the insured all of the premium and administration costs not paid by the federal government. In the case of the hospital insurance program each of the provinces pays a different amount from its consolidated revenue fund into the program. They are free to do the same in the crop insurance program.
One of the points emphasized in many studies of crop insurance in Canada and in

representations on the matter is that provincial governments do not have the financial resources required to back an insurance scheme in case of a severe crop failure or a series of crop failures. This problem is solved in the present bill by the federal government providing loans to provinces to meet indemnity commitments. Provinces would be required to provide all the amounts needed up to $200,000. On any amounts above $200,000 the federal government would loan 75 per cent. It is not unreasonable to consider that provinces could meet these commitments.
This bill calls for an agreement to be signed between the federal government and a provincial government which enters the scheme. The agreement would set out the provisions of the crop insurance scheme to be implemented. Among other things it would limit the insurance coverage to 60 per cent of the average yield in the area. Although the limit of coverage in the United States crop insurance plan is 75 per cent, most insurance coverage is less than this. The Saskatchewan royal commission study on crop insurance stated:
Coverage at 100 per cent-or even 75 per cent- of the long term average yield was found to require premiums above this level-
Ten per cent of the average yield is the level to which reference is made. I continue:
-for the majority of farms. It can be concluded, therefore, that crop insurance offering a high level of coverage is too costly to most Saskatchewan farmers.
The agreement provides, too, that any insurance scheme put into effect will, in so far as is possible to determine, be actuarially sound. Nothing could damage the cause of insurance more than to find, after the scheme had been in effect for a number of years, that the premium rates were inadequate.
Regarding the duration of the agreement, as far as the federal government is concerned the agreement stands for at least ten years. After the expiration of five years the federal government could if it wished terminate the agreement with five years' notice. It is not possible to indicate at this time the details of how crop insurance will work, since there are different ways in which various provinces might implement a crop insurance program. It may be helpful to show how a crop insurance scheme might work, and I underline the word "might".
We will take a hypothetical example, that of Mr. John Smith, farmer, at Simpson, Saskatchewan. This is in the central part of the province. If we assume he is an average
Proposed Crop Insurance farmer in rural municipality No. 281, he will have about 265 acres of wheat.

In the spring Mr. Smith decides to insure his wheat and signs a contract with the provincial crop insurance agency. The range in payments for crop failure would have been from $170 to about $1,750. He would collect the $1,750 in a year like 1937 when there was virtually a complete crop failure. In a year like 1949 he would have collected nearly $1,500. Over the whole period he would have collected $5,600 in payments and would have paid about $4,500 in premiums. The premiums and indemnities will, therefore, greatly exceed any calculation based on the average for the municipality. Proposed Crop Insurance premium costs the farmers' share would be reduced accordingly. In this example it was assumed that the administrative costs of the program were shared equally by the provincial and federal governments. Under this bill the provinces may, if they wish, collect from insured farmers an amount sufficient to cover 50 per cent of administration costs; that is, those administration costs not paid by the federal government.
Taking a particular year for example, say 1960, this farmer would be insured up to 8.4 bushels per acre on his wheat. It may turn out that he would harvest a crop of only 3 bushels per acre. He would receive the difference between the insured amount of 8.4 bushels and the actual yield of 3 bushels, in other words 5.4 bushels per acre. That is what he would be paid for. On 265 acres this would amount to 1,431 bushels which, at a price of $1.25 per bushel, would amount to nearly $1,800. This, of course, is higher than the $1,750 mentioned previously for the crop failure year of 1937 because the price of wheat was lower in 1937.
It is evident, therefore, that a crop insurance plan of this kind will provide farmers with a stability of income which they have never had before. Because this stability is there in bad years, their living standards will not suffer so drastically as in the past, and their investment in the farm business will be protected. Also, with this security, credit facilities will be more readily available. All these things will work to the good of the farmer, his community and the nation as a whole.

When I use the word "adequate" I think that perhaps represents the difference between the policy of the government and that of the Liberal party which was announced at their national convention in January, 1958. The phrase, "adequate financial support from the federal government" was the key part of the Liberal resolution. It was indicated that the Liberal party did support a crop insurance scheme in co-operation with the provinces, and it was also advocated that P.F.A.A. be extended nationally. But the bill means nothing if its terms are not sufficiently attractive to bring in on a national basis not only a comprehensive scheme but most of the provinces of Canada, and I still have very grave doubts that the terms of the bill will be very encouraging to the provinces in this respect.
The minister indicated that there had already been some suggestion that even during this session the province of Manitoba might accept the proposition and introduce a bill. I have very grave doubts about that. I think that was a pretty quick reply. The provincial minister of agriculture actually admitted in the interview that he had not read the bill. But I base my suggestion that they will have a second look at the matter on some of the warnings that were given to the province by the provincial royal commission in 1955. I should like to read a few excerpts which I think will indicate to the house that no government would incur the kind of risks involved in crop insurance without a pretty thorough rather than a casual appreciation of what is involved. On page 76 of the Manitoba commission report I find the following:
A member of the Manitoba crop insurance commission interviewed the manager and other top executives of the F.C.I.C. in Washington, D.C., during the course of this investigation. It was found that these people were unanimous in the view that an area the size of Manitoba, which grows predominantly small grains, subject to similar hazards, would run grave risks in establishing a crop insurance program. They felt there would be a dangerous geographic and crop variety concentration of risks. "No one area can stand alone"-
Another person interviewed in the United States organization is quoted as saying:
In my judgment it would be foolhardy for Manitoba to set up a crop insurance program alone.

There should, theoretically, be some prospect of making it work if all of Canada was in it, but in a state or province there simply would not be enough spreading of risks.
In addition, in the conclusions of the Manitoba royal commission found on page 83 of their report we find the following:
It is not realistic to suppose that a crop insurance program started in a period of good crop years, and limited to Manitoba, would build up the needed reserves. Experience with the United States program has demonstrated that even in periods of high average yield, in small grains areas, heavy indemnity demands are made against the assets of a program. The constant drain against premium assets in an all-risk program successfully frustrates the building up of the enormous reserves in good years that would be required to carry a program over a period of low yield years.
Crop insurance modelled on the F.C.I.C. program (the only operating crop insurance program on the continent) instituted and underwritten by the farmers and government of the province of Manitoba, will not resolve the problem of the instability of farm income. In the event of a series of crop experiences such as have previously occurred in this province, there is no apparently available body of assets or resources substantial enough to maintain a crop insurance program, either voluntary or compulsory, in a solvent state.
I think the minister of agriculture in Manitoba and the provincial treasurer, who is himself the premier, will have a fairly good look at this report. This theme that no one province could go it alone, that it must be on a national basis spreading the risk, is very prominent in all the royal commission reports in the prairie provinces. The Alberta report in 1935 said this:
The Alberta committee said that financial obligations involved and the difficulties of putting a satisfactory crop insurance scheme into operation were subsequently considered too great for any one province to undertake, and, accordingly, the matter was left in abeyance.
In Saskatchewan we had on June 29 a statement as to the need for federal-provincial responsibility, and that the ultimate risk in their view would have to be on the part of the federal government. Even our federal authorities under Mr. Hanson made a report some time ago. He stressed the fact that crop insurance was not practical without a substantial federal responsibility.
I am greatly disappointed, as I said, that the minister-momentarily, I hope-has fixed his mind against the possibility of having this new and important bill investigated by a committee of this house. I point out to him that this legislation runs contrary to the recommendations that were made to the cabinet when they met the major farm organizations in February of this year. The interprovincial farm union on February 16, 1959 said:
We hope that farm organizations will be given an opportunity to study and make recommendations on any proposed plan before it reaches the floor of the house.

It has reached the house but I am sure they would still want an opportunity to make their views known. I suggest to the minister that a refusal to hear these farm organizations and get their views after the terms of the bill are made known is inconsistent with the practice we have followed when major matters of this kind are introduced. For instance, I contrast this procedure with what was done with respect to farm credit legislation. The minister will recall that when amendments were made to the Canadian Farm Loan Act in 1956 we had before us representatives of all the major farm organizations. They were before the parliamentary committee. That procedure was followed again even with respect to minor amendments in 1958. In addition to that, in the case of farm credit we have all had extensive and recent briefs from these organizations. However, that is not true with respect to the matter of crop insurance. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture also met the members of the government early this year, on February 12, and this is what they said:
We heartily approve and endorse the government's intention to introduce a national program oi crop insurance. We believe that an all-risk plan should be made available involving federal and provincial government, as well as producer, participation.
But this is the point.
We further request that in setting up such schemes farm organizations be consulted.
I think it would be an extremely perilous policy to force through this important bill without taking the opportunity of hearing not only these organizations but some of the experts in the provinces, because the provinces are the key to the implementation of anything resulting from this legislation.
I think the Minister of Agriculture has been reasonably fair and modest in outlining the hopes and expectations entertained for this legislation, but I am quite confident that we obtained from the minister of northern affairs on June 29 a fairly good idea of what is going to be said across the land with respect to this untried and unfamiliar legislation. As reported at page 5235 of Hansard the minister of northern affairs said this was another promise made to the people and another promise kept. If this is not something that is going to be accepted by a substantial number of provinces, it is certainly an empty gesture indeed. I think we should know whether or not the terms in the bill are adequate to bring in a substantial number of the people to whom the minister referred.
I want just to read some of the comments that we are going to hear frequently and not only from the minister of northern affairs who is fairly good at making exaggerated 66968-9-353
Proposed Crop Insurance statements. This is the kind of comment we are going to hear. I am quoting from page 5235 of Hansard:
All the way through this report-
He was referring to the Saskatchewan report.
-you sense a great need of people living in a drought area for help in the form of an insurance scheme to guard against some of the risk due to weather. Those people who know something about farming in the dry land areas of the United States and Canada know the great hardships that were suffered by the people in the 30's when there was no such thing as a crop insurance program to provide some help. As a group of people in Canada we were forced to accept relief from the rest of the people of this country. That relief was given in a very generous and Christian fashion but it did something to many of our people that some of us will never forget. That is why there are many in the house today, not the least of whom is the Prime Minister, who led a group of us who said that if we ever had anything to do with running the affairs of the country we would make a tremendous effort to set up some scheme whereby the farmers of western Canada and any other area that needed help could have it on a self-supporting basis so that men's feelings and integrity would be left whole. Therefore this crop insurance legislation is to some of us the fulfilment of a dream long before us.
He emphasized the need of people in drought areas. Mr. Speaker, all the evidence before the royal commissions indicated that these particular people would be excluded from any crop insurance scheme if it was to be actuarially sound, something which the Minister of Agriculture has been emphasizing. I should just like to establish that point by one or two quotations. Let us look at recommendation No. 28 of the Saskatchewan report. They say that in two out of the three areas in Saskatchewan it is not expected that 60 per cent insurance could be provided at premium rates which the farmers could afford to pay. Therefore they would continue to depend on P.F.A.A., the legislation which, from the remarks of the minister of northern affairs, on a relief basis he says this bill will eliminate.

speechtext: The P.F.A.A. will still be there.

speechtext: Of course the P.F.A.A. will still be there, but my point is this. From reading this eloquence of the minister of northern affairs-which I am sure is typical of the speeches he is making in Saskatchewan -one would judge that a majority of the farmers in Saskatchewan are going to find this legislation more attractive than the P.F.A.A. The report itself says-

That is the actual case. The majority of farmers in
Saskatchewan want this.

Proposed Crop Insurance

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
The minister made that point. He quoted from the public hearings referred to in the Saskatchewan report. I assume the minister knows that certainly when there were public hearings, farmers said they would like to have a scheme of crop insurance, and both commissions reported that no representations from farmers indicated that they had any appreciation of the ratio of possible premiums to the benefits they would expect to receive to make an act worth while. In both reports it is very clear indeed that while there was wishful thinking, those interviewed in the public hearings certainly confessed that they could not afford the rates which, if this scheme is to be actuarially sound, would have to be favoured.
I was pleased to read that with respect to insuring wheat alone the record and the experience in the United States had been encouraging. In the United States, according to page 94 of the Saskatchewan commission report, from 1948 through the disastrous wheat year of 1954 the wheat insurance program showed a modest deficit of $4.6 million. During this period nearly $82 million was paid to farmers in the form of wheat indemnities. Nearly all of this, $77 million, was contributed by wheat farmers in the form of premiums. In 1952 the average insured wheat farmer was afforded protection of $15.07 per acre at a cost of $1.25 an acre. This was an average premium cost of less than 7 per cent of coverage. But the point is, as the Minister of Agriculture himself said, that only about 27 per cent or 29 per cent of wheat growers in the United States actually are insured. In Saskatchewan one would judge from reading the commission's report that the premiums would likely be so high that certainly in two of the three major districts where they propose to have a pilot scheme they would find they would have to rely on P.F.A.A. rather than pay the rates which would be necessary if we were to have an actuarially sound system.
Page 16 of the Manitoba report makes reference to possible premiums:
Perhaps one of the most valuable contributions made by those attending the hearings was the indication, that they were able to give, as to how far they, as farmers, would be prepared to go in the payment of premiums to secure what they would consider adequate protection. Although most indicated their desire to have the program self-supporting, with the exception of administrative costs, it soon became evident to the commission that there was little realization of the over-all costs and hazards which would be inextricably bound into any crop insurance program, and that there was a widespread tendency to think in terms of premiums and coverage that would prove, over an extended period of time, to be precariously out of balance in terms of a workable program.


The Saskatchewan commission came to exactly the same conclusion.
I mentioned the other day that it seems from the United States experience that with a voluntary scheme coverage is not very impressive. The Manitoba report at page 41 indicates the scope of effective insurance that has developed down there; and as of 1954, the date indicated in the Manitoba report of 1955, it is said that only one third of a million of producers out of 5.3 million farmers in the United States were insured. In addition they reported that out of a farm crop value of $15 billion, only $400 million was insured. So even there, with a scheme which has been in effect for 20 years, we still have pretty small participation.
I have already made some reference to the claim of the Minister of Agriculture that this is a generous and likely to be an attractive scheme. I do not think that is the case. The commission certainly was very concerned about the ultimate responsibility, notwithstanding that in the end over a long period of time the scheme was supposed to be self-supporting. In the Manitoba report there is the indication that while crop insurance in the United States with respect to wheat was only available from 1939 on, they made a rough calculation, such as the minister did, going back to 1926 and said they had used what they thought a fairly safe premium rate, but when they analysed the likely results over a long period of time from 1926 to 1954 it indicated that in one state alone, the state of North Dakota, the loss would be $100 million. This is the thing which is frightening to the provinces, and I do not think the minister's proposals in this bill are adequate to induce these provinces to get into the scheme, desirable though we all agree it is.
My main point is this. The minister is making a contribution of 50 per cent to administrative expenses. Those are entirely borne by the federal government in the United States. The real contingent liability that he speaks of as being generous and onerous is a loan. If there is disaster the loan eventually has to be paid. In addition, the minister is unilaterally taking upon himself the decision as to what is or what is not actuarially sound. In other words he is in control of the premium rates, and he will not contribute unless he and his advisers are satisfied that over a long period of time it is likely to be actuarially sound.
If he has control of the soundness of the scheme I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that instead of a loan of 75 per cent the federal government, being in the driver's seat on rates, should not make a loan leaving this heavy contingent liability on the provinces to scare

them off acceptance of a scheme of this kind, but rather should assume this liability because they actually are the ones who decide the terms of payment by the producers. That is established, of course, in clause 5 of the bill, where the governor in council has full jurisdiction with respect to this matter of actuarial soundness.
If that is so I do not think the scheme will be very workable or very acceptable to the provinces if they are obliged to repay this substantial risk, without any proviso that it will only have to be paid back if there is some failure or some lack of wisdom on their part in setting up the matter. But the real essence is the actuarial soundness. If the minister is satisfied that it is actuarially sound on a long term basis, I say that it should not be a loan, it should be a guarantee. On that basis we might get the kind of national participation for which one would hope if a scheme of this kind is to be worth while.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the legislation before the house and the method by which it has been introduced can be very strongly and severely criticized. This legislation has been introduced, in the words of the Minister of Agriculture, without discussion with the provinces, without prior consultation and without agreeing to the request of certain provinces that this whole matter should be considered at a formal federal-provincial conference.

speechtext: That is a very interesting comment from the Minister of Agriculture, because I have had on the order paper since June 1, I believe, a motion asking for the production of correspondence with the provinces with reference to the introduction of a crop insurance plan. The minister has failed to produce that correspondence in more than a month, yet in reference to a statement I have made, namely that at least one province has asked for this, he is giving us this bit by bit information which should have been included in the tabling of that return.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit, the minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan asked for this at the last dominion-provincial meeting we had, and he has asked for such conferences on every conceivable agricultural subject at every one of those meetings.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
And, of course, this has been asked by representatives of the farm organizations. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River stated a few moments ago, and read 66968-9-355J
Proposed Crop Insurance quotations in support of his statement, that such a study and such a meeting had been requested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and by other farm organizations. I have in my hand an excerpt from the Moose Jaw Times-Herald of July 6, which reads:
Saskatoon (CP)-The new crop insurance legislation introduced by agriculture minister Harkness should go to the agricultural committee of the commons, says A. P. Gleave, chairman of the interprovincial farm union council.
"I wrote Mr. Harkness twice asking him to refer the bill to the committee, because farm unions and other organizations should have an opportunity to present their views and any recommendations they may have regarding the new legislation," Mr. Gleave said today in a statement.
Although he has had no opportunity yet to study the bill, Mr. Gleave said it appears that under the new act the federal government may actually contribute less to the over-all costs of crop insurance than it did under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
"It is a mistake to rush so important a piece of legislation through the dying hours of the session of parliament," he added.
The Minister of Agriculture has told us that he has had this matter under study for two years-that officials in his department had been studying it for two years- and although the federal government's contribution by way of premiums constitutes only 20 per cent, and the amount of contributions by the provinces and/or the farmers is 80 per cent, the government fails to discuss its general proposals with the provinces.
I think this is an instance in which the federal government is apparently endeavouring to promote the worst kind of federal-provincial relations. I cannot express too strongly my feeling that the government has made a very serious and very grave mistake in the method by which it has introduced this legislation. The provincial treasurer of the province of Saskatchewan has called it, according to a statement in last night's Citizen, "one of the greatest insults ever inflicted on provincial governments by the federal government within my memory." There have been further comments by the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan to which I shall make reference after the lunch hour.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the federal-provincial conference is drawing to a close, that the provincial treasurers are likely to meet this fall, probably in October, and that it is anticipated that from this meeting there will flow a dominion-provincial conference with all the provincial premiers in attendance; a formal conference at an early date, perhaps during the present year. I would suggest that this measure should be stood over, that it should be made part of the agenda of the federal-provincial conference which I understand is slated for October or later this year.

Proposed Crop Insurance This legislation could then be brought out into the open, the views of the premiers and provincial treasurers could be obtained, and we could have a discussion by the governments concerned which must implement this legislation.
The treasurer of the province of Saskatchewan has called this the greatest insult to the provinces in his memory. That is very strong language, the strongest language I can remember since the Prime Minister was on this side of the house castigating the former administration for failing to take the provinces into consultation before announcing government policy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was criticizing the government for not having a federal-provincial conference to deal with the whole question of crop insurance. To show how ridiculous has been the attitude of the government in failing to call such a conference, one needs only mention that there has been going on in this city for the last two days a federal-provincial conference at the provincial treasurers' level. This conference could easily have been extended to include ministers of agriculture. Those ministers of the various provinces could have come to Ottawa. The present conference could have been continued for some time longer in order to work out an agreed crop insurance scheme that would not have the defects of the present bill and that would have had the active and wholehearted co-operation of, I would think, at least the majority of the provinces because they had been consulted and their ideas sought.
This morning the Minister of Agriculture made some critical statements regarding Mr. Robert Moon of the press gallery. I notice that the minister quoted the Winnipeg Free Press. He said, "This is the best known Liberal newspaper in western Canada and I call it as my witness." He then made critical statements regarding a man in the press gallery who is the correspondent for two other well-known daily newspapers in western Canada that have been in the past and are today in general support of the Liberal party.
If one reads on in the article written by Mr. Robert Moon one finds some definition of how farmers under this bill will in fact become ineligible for prairie farm assistance.

Certainly the bombshell in this legislation is that any farmer who wishes to enrol in a crop insurance scheme automatically and by law has his right to obtain benefits under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act taken from him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Is it not a fact that the Saskatchewan royal commission which dealt with crop insurance recommended that if a crop insurance scheme was put into effect, P.F.A.A. levies not be taken and P.F.A.A. payments not be made?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
That was based on the key recommendation of the commission, as I understand it, that a crop insurance scheme should in fact be a federal scheme in the main under which the federal government would accept the major responsibility. If the minister had brought in a measure that complied with the report of the royal commission of which he appears to be in such great support, he would have been accepting the major responsibility instead of endeavouring by this bill to unload the main financial responsibility on the provinces. Any argument as to the recommendations of the Saskatchewan royal commission falls to the ground as far as the minister's point of view is concerned because of the central fact that this government is not complying with the principal recommendation contained in that report.
I have referred to Mr. Robert Moon. Although I am not always in agreement with everything that is reported by him, I think in general Mr. Moon of the press gallery is a conscientious and accurate reporter. I have in my hand a report in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix written by this gentleman, in which he makes reference to certain statements made by the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan, Mr. C. M. Fines. Here is what is said in part:
During his presentation, Mr. Fines also made direct allusion to the recent federal crop insurance proposals when he said that too often the federal government when dealing with such programs had evolved them without consulting the provinces.
Mr. Fines' declarations on centralization were the strongest in this field by Saskatchewan in at least several years at federal-provincial fiscal meetings.
"To do this is to treat the provincial governments as though they were branch offices of the federal government," Mr. Fines said.
''There is a price which must be paid for effective federal-provincial relations and for the willing co-operation of the provincial governments in solving national problems; that price is to take the provinces into the confidence of the federal government even if to do so is to lose some of the political advantage which comes from unilateral action."
This is an example of the failure of the government to consult with the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
may I ask the hon. gentleman a question. From what is he reading and from where did he get it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
I notice the great interest of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I am quoting from a press dispatch from the press gallery sent to the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. While I have not checked with Mr. Fines as to whether or not he made these statements I would think, in spite of the great criticism of the Minister of Agriculture concerning this reporter, that the statements are in fact accurate and represent not only the opinion of Mr. Fines with respect to crop insurance but are an expression of a sound attitude toward federal-provincial relations.
There is another gentleman I should like to quote on the question of federal-provincial relations. I submit that is one of the key questions in the way the crop insurance measure has been handled; because if anything were designed by the federal government to impede federal-provincial relations, to put a gun to the head of the provinces and to act in an arbitrary, unilateral and highhanded manner, then this is indeed a classic example. I should like to quote from the Prime Minister in former days, from a statement he made in this house on July 24, 1956, as reported at page 6370 of Hansard:
I think it is fair to say that the attitude taken by the government at the last conference was an arbitrary one.
In that case there was a conference. I continue:
The government simply said, "These are the terms". No opportunity was given for amendment or for amelioration of any terms. The recipe for a division of taxation was as final as the laws of the Medes and Persians; and how similar that attitude was to the attitude of the government in this house, which is that power makes perfect anything they do. There was no opportunity for negotiation-
And how prophetic these words were in relation to this very bill.
-there was simply the attitude of a feudal lord bringing into being a modern feudalism and laying down the law to the vassals.
Well, this indeed is a very eloquent expression and description of precisely what this government has done and of its attitude in bringing in this legislation. There may have been clandestine discussions with the minister of agriculture of the province of Manitoba; but if the minister of agriculture of Manitoba was brought into some earlier discussions as far as crop insurance is concerned, then apparently he was the only one because there is no evidence that the government discussed
Proposed Crop Insurance these proposals, as it should have discussed them, with the provinces before presenting this detailed measure.
One of the great mistakes that is being made in this legislation is that the federal government has decided to pay only 20 per cent of the premium. In other words the federal government's financial obligation, apart from its share of the administration costs, is 20 per cent of the premium, while under prairie farm assistance legislation, which has been on the statute books of this country since 1939, the federal government's share in practice has been some 50 per cent.
The basis of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is far different from the basis of this legislation. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act applies to three provinces. We in this group have advocated on many occasions that it should be extended to all provinces. It deals with specialized crop areas where crop failure is a hazard. We have advocated that its benefits should be extended to farmers in all provinces; but it is in fact an arrangement between the agricultural producers and the federal government, and without question it has worked for the benefit of the producers who have been allowed to benefit from it.
In the present legislation before the house the federal government, instead of providing for payment of anywhere near 50 per cent, is asking the provinces along with the producers to pay 80 per cent of the cost and the federal government to pay just 20 per cent.
This is not the whole story. Any provincial government coming into this scheme must bear in any given year, according to the legislation, the total losses that occur in that province. Although Saskatchewan is the agricultural province in western Canada, which has experienced the most widespread crop failures and has had paid to its producers the largest amounts, Saskatchewan has not been consulted in any way.
Let us look at the Prairie Farm Assistance Act report for the crop year 1957-58. Let us look back a few years. One finds that in 1954 payments were made to producers in the province of Saskatchewan totalling almost $22 million. If we had a crop insurance program that included the vast majority-which this one does not hope to do-of farmers within that province alone, if the amount of insurance went up to 60 per cent of the average yield then of course the provincial treasury of Saskatchewan could be called upon to pay perhaps $40 million or $50 million in benefits in a single year.
The federal government refuses to share the losses in any way, shape or form. All the federal government proposes to do in this
5596	HOUSE OF
Proposed Crop Insurance legislation is to provide loans to the provinces, and the loans that will be provided by the federal government would apparently carry an extremely high rate of interest. Therefore the federal government, instead of embarking upon an improved, far-reaching program to provide crop failure protection, or crop failure insurance, is endeavouring to transfer a part of the responsibility it has accepted in the past under prairie farm assistance to the provinces which are unable to accept it without risking their financial solvency, because of the great liability and the great charges that may occur under such a scheme.
This program, Mr. Speaker, is also wanting in that the plan is of little or no benefit to producers who suffer most from crop failure; it is of little or no benefit to producers who live in the high risk areas. As a matter of fact, under this program the government apparently has a desire to divide the farmers of Canada into two classes, namely those who live in high risk areas who cannot afford to come under the proposed scheme, and those who do not face the same type or the same degree of crop failure risks, farmers who operate the more productive land areas which can be covered by such a proposed plan.
How we have heard members opposite during the course of this session say they were interested in the small farmer; they were interested in the farmer with a low income; they were interested in the farmer whose production was not as high as that of some other farmers; they in fact were interested in the farmer who needed the greatest amount of consideration. Well, under this legislation farmers in areas facing the greatest degree of crop failure risk will not be able to obtain in any substantial measure whatever benefit or whatever protection may be provided.
On many occasions the minister has referred to the Saskatchewan royal commission report on crop insurance. If this legislation is designed according to the examples that are set forth in that royal commission report then it is going to create many of the problems that prairie farm assistance has been endeavouring to overcome for many years. For example, in the insurance proposal set forth it says there shall be a premium unit, there shall be crop delivery points, and that farmers within that area will pay the same premium. The Minister of Agriculture is sufficiently well acquainted with western Canada to know that from farm to farm productivity varies very substantially within an area where the farmers market their grain at a central delivery point; and to calculate premiums even on the basis of this type of


unit is less fair, I suggest, than the prairie farm assistance method of collecting 1 per cent of deliverable production as it goes to market.
I do not think that is as serious as the further provision in these examples having to do with an indemnity unit. If the minister wishes to correct my interpretation of these examples I will be very pleased if he will do so. But as I interpret the calculations in these examples the indemnity unit is the same area as the premium unit, and in order to ascertain the premium that would be required in this unit it is assumed that the indemnity is paid on the unit. We are all aware of the great criticism in the past when areas for payment under prairie farm assistance were substantially larger than they are now, and farmers complained that although they had a crop failure they were unable to get assistance while some of their neighbours who were in a unit where payment was made and who had a relatively good crop nevertheless obtained prairie farm assistance. If the indemnity unit is to be as it is set forth in these examples then payment will not be made on an individual basis at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member needs to go any further along that line. I think I made it quite clear that what is envisaged here is individual crop insurance, not on a unit basis nor an area basis.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
I understand that is the position of the minister, but I am referring to the examples set forth by the Saskatchewan royal commission on which their rates for premiums and indemnity are calculated and which have been used by the minister. What I am pointing out is that in these calculations they have not calculated payment on an individual basis but on an area basis. I accept the minister's statement, and may I say that I did not think differently; but I suggest this means that if in actual practice payments are made on an individual basis, then the premium required to meet such payments will be higher than the premium set forth in the examples given in the Saskatchewan royal commission report.
The legislation before the house is very loosely worded. Under this legislation the government can-indeed, I take it the government intends to do so-make agreements with the provinces that are not in any general standard form at all but probably will differ very much in important aspects. Mr. Speaker, after listening to the last two members who have spoken on this subject I have only one observation to make. Perhaps it is not original but I think it is appropriate. Forgive them, Mr. Speaker, for they know not what they say. I should like to deal with the subject of crop insurance for a change, and I am sure that hon. members here today would like to have an opportunity to discuss the bill now before the house rather than to ramble on discussing provincial issues and attempting to lay the foundation for a provincial election.
In order to put the whole matter in its proper perspective I want to read from the report of the dominion-provincial economic conference of 1950, which dealt with the subject and made some recommendations with respect to crop insurance. The report goes on in introducing the subject-and it is the introduction that I want to read-to say this:
The application of crop insurance as an income-maintenance device introduces many complex implications. It can be made comparable to social security, unemployment insurance or calamity insurance, (flood, fires, etc.) depending on the objectives of particular crop insurance programs. Furthermore, it can be a partial application of each of these types of program (in terms of the proportion of income insured). It may assume, in its various garbs, the status of a self-supporting or subsidized program and participation can be voluntary or compulsory. All of these choices depend on primary objectives adopted and on an over-all conception of the functions and uses of crop insurance.
In this study the major assumption adopted is that crop insurance is a self-liquidating type of insurance based on sound actuarial data. As such, crop insurance is related directly to production rather than considerations of welfare or security. It should be designed to treat individual operators facing similar risks in a similar fashion without subsidizing inefficiency or penalizing efficiency. Welfare payments, where necessary, should be dealt with outside the scheme of crop insurance and should be treated as a social security scheme rather than related primarily to productivity.
Crop insurance has been a fairly lively issue in Canada for approximately two decades and particularly so in western Canada. Considerable

Proposed Crop Insurance effort has been spent from time to time in presenting arguments pro and con various proposals. In many cases crop insurance has been overemphasized as a solution to the very fundamental problem of instability in agriculture. It is essential that this too be seen in its proper perspective. Taken by itself, crop insurance is merely a device to take a portion of production which has taken place unevenly over a period of years and to return that part or premium in such a fashion that the producers' annual yields approach a figure which represents a long-term average annual production or some percentage of that production. It is necessary, therefore, that the average production represent a suitable level of income for the individual farmer. Unfortunately, there are many instances throughout Canada where even the guarantee of an annual production approximating a long-term average will not, in all cases, result in a satisfactory return. Paradoxically, these areas need insurance most but are least able to afford the premium rate necessary to pay for a proper level of insurance. Areas other than these have not as great a need for insurance but can, nevertheless, use it to advantage since it offers them cheap protection. These observations seem to indicate that a concerted attack on more fundamental factors will have to be made before crop insurance can be successfully applied in those areas which need stability most.
I might say that this report, as I stated before, was drawn up in 1950. Since this government has come to office it has dealt with those aspects of instability that it has been necessary to deal with in order to complement a crop insurance program and to ensure the success of crop insurance.
One of the main criticisms that have been levelled at the P.F.A.A. over the years has been the fact that some farmers who have made contributions to the scheme since 1939 have been unsuccessful in collecting indemnities or payments when they have suffered crop failures. In suggesting that we should continue with an expanded program of P.F.A.A., as the hon. member for As-siniboia has done, what is he actually contemplating? It seems to me that what he is saying is this, and I am sure he would not make an effort to sell this type of insurance to a householder or to a person interested in life insurance. What it actually means is that it is a type of insurance policy that says you will not collect a nickel's worth of insurance when your house burns down unless 18 of the houses on the same street burn down at the same time; or that your wife will not collect a nickel's worth of insurance when you die unless 18 of your neighbours die the same year. I am sure that he or anyone else would have difficulty in attempting to sell that type of insurance to a home owner or to a person who is interested in life insurance.
I have no criticism of the purpose of P.F.A.A. when it was first brought into being. It was enacted to deal with a situation that existed in the thirties, namely that of drought. In dealing with that particular situation,

where invariably you would have a wide area affected, it could conceivably cover most of the farmers in the areas stricken. However, the situation that has existed, particularly in the province of Manitoba, has been one of local failure where there has not been an opportunity for a farmer suffering local crop losses to participate in benefits or to receive payments under P.F.A.A.

However, I think this is beside the point. What this bill is doing -and I think this is the important thing and that the point has been missed-or what this government is doing is providing an opportunity for a provincial government to draw up a program of crop insurance

suited to the particular needs of that province, and permitting the farmers in the area to make some contribution to the development of that program.
It has been stated by most of the commissions or bodies that have been studying this particular subject that one province attempting to go into a crop insurance program by itself would in all probability find itself in difficulties if it had a succession of failures in the early part of the program. Therefore the recommendations of the Manitoba commission, the Saskatchewan commission and of many of the reports that have been drawn up have been to the effect that the federal government must participate in this program. On no occasion has any of these commissions suggested that the federal government has to be in complete control of the development of the entire program.
What we are doing is simply providing financial assistance to the provinces in the event that they have crop failures in the initial stages of their program. In addition to this the government is paying 50 per cent of the administrative costs. The federal government is doing, in addition, something that has been suggested by no commission in connection with this program, in that the government is going to pay 20 per cent of the premiums of the farmers.
This is quite important. This suggestion has been criticized by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I have not been in this house too long, but those of us who have been here during the last two years know full well that it would not matter if the government paid 250 per cent of the premiums, the hon. member would still find something about which to complain.
I might say that I was in Manitoba just two weeks ago, and my attention has been called to the fact that the press gallery noted my absence on one particular night. The farmers arranged a series of meetings for me to attend, and at each of those meetings there was a considerable amount of interest in crop insurance. Proposed Crop Insurance program. I did not find, amongst those farmers the attitude that was expressed by the hon. member for Assiniboia, that they are afraid to pay the premium rates. As indicated in this report of the Manitoba commission, the farmers are anxious to stand on their own feet. All they are looking for is an opportunity to take out a crop insurance policy so they can be protected from the hazards with which they are confronted from time to time.
Although we all know these things are not always perfect, I am satisfied that the bill is acceptable to the province of Manitoba. I am satisfied that as a result of this legislation we will have crop insurance in the province next year. I take a great deal of pleasure in participating, just briefly, in this debate. I should like to congratulate the minister upon bringing this measure forward and upon having the courage, despite all the procrastination that has occurred in connection with crop insurance over the years, to introduce a measure providing an opportunity for the provinces to develop programs suitable to the needs of their farmers. Under the plan provided in the bill, the federal government provides for the payment of contributions and the grants of loans to provinces that set up their own crop insurance scheme. It is the same standard formula that is used when it is a question of distributing the economic and social responsibilities between provincial and federal governments. That method-one that is often referred to-is considered a socializing one in certain quarters. Besides, it requires, on the part of the governments, continuous supervision together with considerable expense and, furthermore, it interferes with farmers' freedom.
Would it not be wiser to try to find a new formula which would eliminate all those drawbacks?
Mr. Speaker, having given this matter a great deal of thought, the idea occurred to me of submitting an altogether personal plan that I would ask the minister to kindly take into consideration.
That plan is to have a crop insurance scheme managed by an organization that would represent a majority of the farmers of a province, whenever the province concerned would not feel it would be advantageous to follow that federal policy for reasons of autonomy or other reasons. In the province of Quebec we have important organizations which represent farm people quite well, just as there are such organizations in other provinces. One such organization which has acquired a great experience in the field of insurance and actuarial science, while constantly keeping in touch with farm people, is the "Assurance-Vie Desjardins".
This company has only ten years experience, yet it already has close to half a billion dollars of insurance in force.
Other organizations doing a good job of representing the agricultural class are: La Cooperative Federee, in the economic field, and the Union des Cultivateurs Catholiques, in the professional field.
Both organizations have several years of experience in the insurance field, and I have no doubt that if the government came up with a definite proposal, they would consider it.
The administration of a crop insurance scheme could not be more secure than in the hands of those organizations, because, better than any other organization, they are familiar with the needs of their members and they already have a trained staff and experience in various types of risks.
The minister will object that the government cannot invest funds in a service without having control over expenditures. I recognize that. However, would it not be possible, after having the matter thoroughly investigated by economists, trained actuaries and

the interested parties, to find a satisfactory formula? I for one am convinced it could be done.
Over the years, successive governments have yielded to popular pressure for the provision of various social and economic security services.
Nowadays, workers, farmers and manufacturers cannot do a thing without looking to the government for guidance or remedial action.
Farmers, in the past, have always been able to look after their own responsibilities, and I see no reason why we should not trust them to do the same in the matter of crop insurance.
We regret, however, that the minister has not seen fit to introduce this legislation earlier, so as to enable members, farm organizations, experts in this field, and also the provinces, to give it a thorough study and put forward some fair and considered suggestions.

Proposed Crop Insurance because of the complications of crop insurance and the difficulties that I can well understand that action was delayed from year to year. However, I do want to make five points. I am not going to be repetitious.
First of all, I want to inform the house that crop insurance has been a plank in the C.C.F. agriculture program for many years. As a matter of fact, it is plank No. 3 at the present time. It reads as follows:
A system of crop insurance to protect farmers against crop failure due to conditions beyond their control.
This is supported by the C.C.F., and on that account we support the principle of crop insurance. I am very sorry that in legislation of this type which for its successful administration requires, in my opinion, the closest co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) has not had consultations with the ministers of agriculture of the provinces or representatives of those provinces. I think that is essential before there can be sucess in the administration of any legislation of this type. In my opinion the whole success of this legislation is founded on successful dominion-provincial co-operation in this very important matter.
I want also to protest the late introduction of the bill. This legislation was mentioned in the throne speech. I believe it would have been far better if this legislation had been introduced earlier in the session. To introduce it in the dying days of the session, in my opinion, is not good enough. I think this is a sound criticism and the minister knows that my criticisms are usually quite sound. If it had been presented earlier in the session and then sent to a committee-we are very sorry that the bill is not being sent to the agriculture committee-the members of the house could have studied the bill and given it further consideration and the representatives of farm organizations could have appeared before the committee and expressed their views of this very complicated and difficult piece of legislation.
Before the bill was finally drafted and presented to this house there should have been the closest consultation between the representatives of the various provinces and the national farm organizations in Canada. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are very sorry that it is not the intention of the minister to have this bill referred to the agriculture committee of the house.
In conclusion, I simply want to ask the minister, to plead with him, in view of the great importance of this legislation and of
[Mr. Herridge.l
its peculiar nature which requires co-operation from all those interested in its administration, through governments, through producer organizations to farmers themselves, to refer this bill to the agriculture committee and give the farmers' organizations of Canada an opportunity to appear before the committee and express their views, to make suggestions, and so on.
I think it is only fair to realize that this is experimental legislation. With the best of intentions, with all the consultation among the provinces and the farmers' organizations and the understanding of the farmers themselves, it at best can only be experimental legislation. Experience will no doubt indicate that there must be amendments, adjustments and improvements. On that account, we say that this is one bill that should have been presented to the provinces concerned. It should have been brought to this house at an earlier date; it should have been sent to the agriculture committee so as to ensure as far as humanly possible co-operation from all people interested, with a view to making it a success to the advantage of the farmers of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the second reading of this bill which provides for a very important part of our national agricultural policy for Canada I think I should put before the house some of the behind the scenes issues that are being fought here. I am not going to deal with the details of the particular clauses of the bill and discuss their pros and cons. It has been my hope over the past year or so that when the bill was presented to the house we would consider it soberly and with the idea that we are moving into a field that is brand new to any government in Canada. This has not been the case. We were suddenly confronted with the violent position taken by the leader of the C.C.F. party in the house that the bill was bad for Canada and particularly for western Canada.
The house cannot understand the significance of this speech unless we look at a little of the background of the whole situation respecting crop insurance in so far as it affects us in the province of Saskatchewan. Before I embark on that particular part of my remarks I should like to say that I am not going to talk a great deal about the Liberal position. We recognize their situation in the house in that they do not have many members from the farm areas, particularly from western Canada, who know of the long fight we have had for crop insurance. Their attitude is typical. The suggestion I got from them was that we should be very cautious and should approach this matter very carefully.

We can understand this attitude. Back in 1919 the Liberals proposed a health insurance scheme. We finally put it into effect in 1959. That is a period of 40 years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Nonsense.
