speechtext:
The Liberals took a very cautious attitude in that regard and now the suggestion is that we are going a little too fast with crop insurance. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) quoted the Winnipeg Free Press today and I should like to quote this comment with regard to the contribution of the federal government which appeared in an editorial in the issue of July 2:
Certainly the payment of half of the administration costs and one-fifth of premium costs will be interpreted by many people as another government hand-out to the farmer.
So the Liberal position, as I understand it, is that we are going too fast in meeting the problems of agriculture and that we are giving a handout to the farmers of western Canada and farmers generally throughout Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Nonsense. You just will not disclose what your partners think about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: This attitude of the Liberal party indicates that we are moving too fast. They would like to take 40 years to carry out the job as they have done in the past.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
On the other hand, by contrast the government has recognized the need of agriculture in all parts of Canada. We have acted immediately because I think to have brought in as much agricultural legislation within two years as we have indicates the urgency that we consider this matter has. We realize that the crop insurance bill is new legislation but, Mr. Speaker, why criticize the legislation until it has been given a chance?
All this legislation involves is permission for the government to make agreements with the provinces whereby they can consider the individual needs of their particular parts of Canada and provide an actuarially sound crop insurance scheme in order to try to remove the effect of the ups and downs of the weather for farmers in every part of Canada. No position of criticism can be taken today that cannot be called irresponsible because not one agreement has been worked out. We want the bill passed so that those provinces that want to institute crop insurance to give some stability of income to their farmers will have a chance to propose
Proposed Crop Insurance their schemes and then we can work out a co-operative agreement between us.
The province of Manitoba has already indicated its willingness to propose a scheme and to enter into an agreement with us on a co-operative crop insurance program. I would suggest, in line with what the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has said, that there is a need to look at the bill on the basis of the needs of agriculture. I would suggest to him with equal seriousness that such legislation has been looked at, examined and discussed by farm organizations and political parties for at least 25 years to my knowledge. Proposals have been put forward and debated but the fact is that very few organizations have had the facts and figures on which to base a crop insurance scheme.
The only experience we have to go on is that with the spring wheat crop insurance scheme in the United States, the figures in the Manitoba crop insurance report and the figures from P.F.A.A. experience over a period of 20 years. On the basis of this experience we are confident that we can put forward an actuarially sound program that the farmers will support because they do not want relief but simply the chance to help themselves.
In the preliminary periods of the study of crop insurance most of the reports that were issued were pessimistic because they did not have the basic information which we think we now have on which to base a crop insurance plan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Where did that come from?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
So you can
understand why the early reports took a pessimistic attitude. The latest study we have is volume 9 of the report of the royal commission on agriculture and rural life in Saskatchewan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: We have all quoted that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
This royal
commission was appointed in 1952. It consisted of five people picked from the province of Saskatchewan who the C.C.F. government thought were capable of understanding the complexities of the problem and of issuing a report for the guidance of the province of Saskatchewan which has a C.C.F. government. The royal commission was established because the situation was such particularly in Saskatchewan that there had to be some form of coherent program put before governments on which they could act.
In our membership in this house, just as in the membership of the Saskatchewan legislature, you would not expect to find
5606	HOUSE OF
Proposed Crop Insurance people with the experience and the time to deal with this complex question and propose constructive programs. The royal commission has published its report in 14 volumes and it has been a matter of considerable interest to me why these reports were never quoted either in the legislature of Saskatchewan, whose taxpayers paid over half a million dollars to get them, or by the C.C.F. members in the House of Commons at Ottawa in the 1957 and 1958 sessions or in the present session. The first time I heard a member of the C.C.F. party quote these reports was in this debate.
As I read the speech of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) he definitely left the impression in the house that the bill before us now is contrary to the recommendations of this report. That feeling which he left in the house, and which is also noted by any person who reads his first speech, is contrary to the facts. The only way in which we have differed from the recommendations in the report is that, first of all, we have gone further than the report recommends in the sense that we have offered to any province a scheme whereby they can bring their farmers into a crop insurance program and, second, we have not asked that the scheme be compulsory as the report recommends.
As I said in my remarks on the resolution, to those of us who have gone through the galling experience of nine years of drought where 80 per cent to 90 per cent of our people were forced to their knees and compelled to take relief, this is the type of thing we thought was a practical approach to one of the problems facing agriculture in a drought area. We therefore pledged ourselves that if we ever reached the position where we could do something about it we would bring in some form of crop insurance in order to give the farmers some opportunity to pay an insurance premium so they would not be ruined by these years of poor crops or in the case of some other catastrophy.
Therefore when I hear in this house the suggestion that it is wrong for me to speak of these things, my mind goes back to the day when the freight cars pulled up to our small towns in Saskatchewan and brought us tons of dried codfish. At that time the farmers lined up to the doors of those boxcars to take those big flat things we had never seen before. We were told, "This is to feed yourselves with." I well recall that in our district we heard that there was a farmer about 60 miles away who came from New Brunswick and who knew how to cook these things. We thought they were snowshoes. This farmer made a big reputation for himself simply by giving the advice that before


you eat the things, you boil them or soak them in water for twenty-four hours. I remember a carload of apples coming in from Ontario and I remember clothing being distributed.
It is bad enough when sometimes a calamity hits a community by way of fire or earthquake and a few thousand people receive help through the generosity of their neighbours and their fellow citizens. But when a whole area of a country feels this not just for one year but year after year for seven or eight years, you can understand the feeling with which we approach this bill. Now what happens? I think I can say with some proof that over the years in Saskatchewan every political party has supported the idea of crop insurance. I can say with complete accuracy that in the debate in the legislature in Regina this February on the speech from the throne C.C.F. speakers supported crop insurance and Liberal speakers supported crop insurance. I have clippings here to demonstrate the truth of what I say. This one is dated February 17 and is from the Moose Jaw Times-Herald. It is a Canadian Press dispatch:
A.L.S. Brown (CCF-Bengough) told the Saskatchewan legislature Monday this province Is willing to take part in a crop insurance policy with the federal government.
And so on right down the line. Later on in another debate there were 16 speakers spoke. This is the whip of the Liberal party speaking and this is a quotation from the Star-Phoenix of February 27, 1959. It reads as follows:
He favoured crop insurance, to help contend the "natural hazards," and some form of farm credit to aid young farmers get started.
Here is a legislator from Saskatchewan representing a rural riding, the whip of the Liberal party, joining with the C.C.F. speaker, Mr. Brown, one of the most experienced members the C.C.F. have in the legislature, calling for crop insurance and help for young farmers. That is exactly what this government is doing. It is trying to meet the farmers' needs all across Canada, something which is supported by political parties of every stripe in Canada, yet we meet this sort of attack that we get from the hon. member for Assiniboia.
Naturally enough, I was suspicious of what was going on. I wondered about this contradictory position. I knew that all these members of the royal commission supported crop insurance and they still do. I knew that Mr. Nollet, minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan, had expressed support for crop insurance a few months ago. I knew that Mr. Brown, C.C.F. member for Bengough, had

been willing to co-operate. I have seen the resolution passed by associations over the years and right up to this very last year. Then all of a sudden we get this doom talk by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I have therefore been putting two and two together. We heard the Minister of Agriculture say today some harsh words about a reporter in the press gallery for having written a story that went all across Saskatchewan in three papers, I understand, dealing with this matter of crop insurance. This report which is dated June 30, 1959 from the Regina Leader-Post on the front page bears the heading "Prairie Farm Assistance Cancelled". Sometimes we blame these headlines on the headline writers who are different people from the men who write the stories. But the opening paragraph clears away that little matter. This is what the opening paragraph says:
The cancellation of prairie farm assistance emerged as a surprise package in the new federal government crop insurance proposals announced Monday afternoon in the commons.
The Minister of Agriculture has made it absolutely clear that this is completely false. Yet the hon. member for Assiniboia stands up in the house and says that this reporter is not only conscientious but is accurate. Reading on in this story a little further, I read this:
In the debate C.C.F. house leader Hazen Argue heaped praise on the P.F.A. legislation and on its Commons instigator, former agriculture minister Gardiner.
I have read through that speech twice and I have not been able to find that the hon. member for Assiniboia mentioned Mr. Gardiner. Where did Moon get hold of this doom? There must have been collaboration outside of this house that is not recorded in Hansard. I asked the hon. member today to quote what he is reading from. I saw him reading from the transcript of one of these pieces of paper that roll through the linotype machine that transmits a message across the country and he says, "I obtained this from the press gallery". It is my conviction that if you are reading it at the very moment the thing is not printed yet. But the hon. member for Assiniboia reads these accurate reports to the house.
Why this alliance between gloom and doom? He praises Mr. Gardiner. All you have to do is praise Mr. Gardiner and then you are put on a high pedestal in the Leader-Post in Regina. Mr. Gardiner is a fairly doughty little man and he does not need much protection from the hon. member for Assiniboia. Why this sudden lovemaking between these two people? I will leave that matter to your imagination, Mr. Speaker. I can go on and read through these clippings and point out
Proposed Crop Insurance the inaccuracies. I would suggest to the hon. member for Assiniboia that if Moon is as accurate as he claims, let him print this fact. I say in this house that this royal commission report is repudiated in effect by the hon. member for Assiniboia in his remarks in this house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: It is repudiated by this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
I say flatly that the royal commission report is accepted by this government with these two differences. One is that we did not bring in the compulsory feature and the second is that we went farther than the royal commission report recommended. They wanted just to have three experimental units to start with. There is nothing to stop the Saskatchewan government from making an agreement with regard to these three experimental units. We simply made it possible to do it all over the province all at once. I should like to suggest that if the reporter is conscientious and accurate in reporting what goes on in this house let him tell the people of Saskatchewan why the C.C.F. are really opposed to crop insurance, why they supported it back in February and oppose it in July. I will suggest to you the reason, Mr. Speaker. It is the same reason that gripped them a year ago February. When we brought in the farm stabilization act they saw their death knell being rung. They see the end of the C.C.F. party in the west because this is going to be the first step in removing the causes of friction between the government and the farmers. The C.C.F. would have nothing left about which to howl.
They called the farm price stabilization bill every name of which they could think in this house and get away with. The remarks of the former hon. member for Springfield, Mr. Schulz, still ring in my ears. I took those same remarks made by Mr. Schulz and read them to farm audiences across the prairies during the last election. The result was that Mr. Schulz, -and his extreme remarks, are no longer in the house. I am suggesting that the real fear of the C.C.F. at this moment over the very fine start that we have made in this very complex problem of crop insurance is that they see us removing another great fear of the farmer of these sudden catastrophes that hit him. The result is that they have one less thing for which they can hammer the federal government and by which the provincial government of Saskatchewan hopes to avoid its responsibilities.
Let Mr. Moon tell the people of Saskatchewan that is the real reason for the C.C.F. party's change of opinion at this time. It is not because the people of Saskatchewan do

Proposed Crop Insurance not want crop insurance, it is because the C.C.F. are afraid if we put in crop insurance the C.C.F. government will be caught short. They know that if this bill goes into effect before this parliament closes the Saskatchewan legislature will have to act. There is only another year before that provincial government must meet the people and they do not want to have to enact something that will remove grievances the farmer has because they want these grievances with which to pound the head and shoulders of the federal government. I would suggest to the hon. member for Assiniboia, as I have suggested before, that his exaggerations in this house have ruined his effect on the house as a serious member. If he supported crop insurance in the past, he should not turn his back on ten or fifteen years of espousing the thing in order to save a provincial party. He should think of the farmers of this country first. The C.C.F. party knows that the next piece of legislation to come forward is equally potent medicine in helping to cure the ills that beset the farmers.
As I read these clippings that have come into my hands within the last few days, and as I hear the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan calling this bill an insult to the government of Saskatchewan, I wonder what precipitated this somersault. Mr. Fines' reputation is unassailable. He has been in office 15 years and he has shown a surplus of $12 million or $15 million every year. He has steadily reduced the debt of Saskatchewan until it is now in the neighbourhood of $20 million. Every time the C.C.F. members talk about something to help the people of Saskatchewan he says, "Oh, no; before I leave this office I want Saskatchewan to be absolutely clear of debt." Has this government ever let a few dollars of debt stop it from doing what was necessary, either in the way of old age pensions or something for the workingman or the farmer? We see our duty and we do it. We ask the people of Canada to support us in this type of legislative action which gets at the real problems with which the people of this country are faced. Mr. Fines has a good reputation, and yet he tells the C.C.F. members, you will have to hold off until we get all these debts cleared off before we do anything.
If I were in the provincial government of Saskatchewan and I knew the majority of the people had expressed their desire for crop insurance I would be prepared to let the debt remain for another year in order to give the people some security so that they could sleep at night without worrying what might happen if a disaster from weather hit them. I have said enough here, Mr. Speaker, to make it clear that this opposition to the
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1

bill is opposition born of desperation in attempting to enable the C.C.F. government to avoid putting in crop insurance legislation. On that ground, I would suggest that hon. members here should not play any part in delaying this bill in any way just to save a political party some embarrassment. You can have all the committees you like but you cannot do a more thorough job than has been done in all these reports, and particularly this one which represents a four-year study. Every time there has been a meeting before, the lack of adequate figures has always been a pressing problem. This report does make an attempt to give us the figures, and with the figures we have collected from other places I think we have a chance of making this crop insurance plan succeed. If it does succeed, then those who are members of the house at this time may say, we did help the farmers move toward a position of self-help from which they can attain reasonable equality with the rest of Canada. Every one of us should be proud to be here and support such a bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there were some observations in the speech to which we have just listened which I think merit some comment from those of us who sit in the official opposition. Of course, the quarrel between the minister of northern affairs and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) which has obviously taken on heat today, interesting as it is, is one that can only be resolved by those two gentlemen. I would not want in any way to add to the nature of this dispute; I would not want to add to its intensity, although I admit it is a very interesting controversy. I repeat, it is one which can properly be resolved only by these two gentlemen.
But in the course of his remarks the minister did make one or two observations which I think marred his political endeavour today. I think what he has said, and I say this in a kindly way to the minister, was largely in the nature of a political diatribe which did not add very much to the information of this house. It was a rather acrimonious and vigorous defence of the administration, and from that point of view of course the minister's participation is understandable. He said that the attitude of those of us sitting in the official opposition, while not one of opposition to the measure was one that could hardly be regarded as full support. We were suggesting caution; we were suggesting care; and the consequences of our advice were that the measure would be delayed unnecessarily. Of course, the hon. gentleman must accept responsibility, along with his colleagues, for the introduction of this measure at this late stage of the session.

There is an obligation on the part of the opposition to give careful attention to all matters put forward by the government, and we would not be doing our duty if we did not examine this bill with all of the thoroughness we could possibly command. It was for this reason we suggested it would be advisable for the minister to agree to send this bill to a committee so that it could be carefully studied, so that there would be an opportunity given to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, to the interprovincial farm union and to the provincial governments themselves to indicate to the committee their feelings in the matter. The provincial governments could indicate how much participation could be expected by provincial governments. We could learn the view of the various farm organizations. Certainly, this is not an unreasonable proposal. If the government decides that that is not the kind of thorough investigation they want, well then there is of course nothing that we on this side can do.
The government has a huge majority, and if it wishes to take a particular course there is nothing that can be done, but surely the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) does not expect us to fail in the performance of our obligations as we see them. One of these is to point out that one of the weaknesses of this measure is that it is not receiving the kind of hearing that a measure of this sort should receive. This is a measure which depends for its success on the attitude taken by the provinces. Since there is not going to be any feature of compulsion about the measure, it will depend solely for its success on the co-operation and the support which it will receive from farmers from one end of Canada to the other. The minister, when he spoke, spoke only of the prairie provinces; he keeps forgetting that there are farmers in other parts of Canada, too, and they should have the advantage of this or any other similar legislation.
Whatever weaknesses in this measure become apparent later on will probably prompt suggestions that those weaknesses could have been eliminated if a proper study which we propose had been accepted by the government. The minister of northern affairs said it was not necessary to have any further discussions on this matter. I think he said that the federation of agriculture-and if I am wrong in this the hon. gentleman will correct me-had already given an indication of its position with regard to this measure. If that is so, I wish the minister could have given us more particulars. It would be interesting to know whether or not the federation of agriculture has carefully considered the provisions of this bill. It will be interesting
Proposed Crop Insurance to know whether the minister had acquainted the council of the federation, not with all the details but with the broad terms of this legislation. We do know that the interprovincial farm union, in a statement I saw the other day in the newspapers, has expressed some concern over this particular measure. I do not want to call that a condemnation of the bill, but certainly it would be desirable and helpful if, in committee, we were able to interrogate members of the interprovincial farm union not because they would oppose the principle of the bill, and not because we oppose the principle of the bill, but because the principle behind this bill, being sound, deserves to be incorporated in legislation which would be the most effective possible. The answers to the questions we keep putting to the minister-questions about the attitude of the provinces-do not convince us that this bill, good as it is in its present form, will satisfy the expectations which have been raised.
The minister of northern affairs said that this government was not like the Liberal government, it did not wait 22 years to bring in crop insurance, and it did not wait all the time the Liberal government did before bringing in hospital insurance. Of course, that struck a personal note and that is one of the reasons which brought me to my feet. I will tell the minister the differences between Liberal governments and Conservative governments. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that his government would bring in a comprehensive scheme of crop insurance. We do not have before us a bill which represents a comprehensive scheme of crop insurance. The undertaking and assurance given by the Prime Minister in this matter certainly has not been met by this bill. When we proposed a system of hospital insurance, it did take some time. It took some time because we could not possibly proceed with it unless we had the co-operation of the provinces, and we did not propose to put on the statute books of this parliament a measure of that nature unless we knew we would have the support of a sufficient number of provinces who would come into the scheme. Prior to the introduction of that measure, unlike the present administration in regard to the bill now before us, we did have conferences with the provinces, we did talk this question over with them, and we did reconcile our differences. Finally, we were able to bring forward an act which has won the support of eight, and possibly nine, of the provincial governments.
Moreover, the minister of northern affairs was a little confused. He began to say that they had brought in not only crop insurance

Proposed Crop Insurance but hospital insurance, forgetting, of course, that the hospital insurance act, which had been preceded by consultations with provincial and voluntary bodies, was placed on the statute books by a Liberal government at a time when the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent was prime minister of this country. It seems to be necessary to remind some hon. gentlemen of that fact, and apparently it is necessary to remind the minister of northern affairs with regard to what really took place. I suggest to him that if he looks on the hospital insurance measure as one which occasions a comparison between the techniques of the two governments he might well have observed the superior technique employed in the matter of the hospital insurance program.
That bill was, as I say, preceded by conferences with the provinces, conferences with hospital associations, with medical bodies and so on whereas, according to the words of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), this particular bill has been preceded by no consultation whatsoever either with the provinces or with the various farm organizations. It is true that about a year ago the minister had a meeting with the provincial ministers of agriculture to discuss crop insurance, as he said, in a very general way, but the particular proposals embodied in this bill were, according to his own admission, never discussed with any provincial government or farm organization. Despite that, this government persists in denying parliament the normal process of investigation and assessment, namely referring this matter to the committee on agriculture.
The minister of northern affairs in his very interesting discourse this afternoon spoke of the body which was set up in Saskatchewan in 1952, the royal commission on agriculture and rural life. He said that no one had referred at all during the course of the debate to the report made by that body. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), who was the first to speak for us in this group, did refer to that report, and in fairness to the hon. member for Assiniboia I may say that I well remember that he did so as well. Of course, all the way through this debate, this report which I have in my hand was referred to by hon. members, and why the minister of northern affairs who spoke of this as the most monumental study of its kind in Canada should yet have refrained from referring to some of its very definite recommendations is very difficult to understand.
This bill does not come forward in full conformity with the assurances given by the Prime Minister. This bill is not a generous bill. This bill deserves support because it


establishes the principle of crop insurance. But I say to hon. gentlemen opposite that if they really want to live up to their election promises, if they really want to do something that is going to have the most efficient results, they should unhesitatingly have taken the provinces into their confidence. I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that when we come back to parliament it will be interesting to find out whether any more than one province will have taken advantage of this measure. I ask the Minister of Agriculture now: will the province of Ontario take advantage of it? Will the three western provinces, other than Manitoba take advantage of it? Will British Columbia, or will the maritime provinces, or will the province of Quebec take advantage of it? I ask the Minister of Agriculture a second time in this debate, is there any indication that he can give us as to the likelihood of their acceding to the proposition embodied in this bill?
We were told this morning that the province of Manitoba is going to come in but the Minister of Agriculture admitted in answer to a question put to him by me that the province of Manitoba had indicated last December its intention of introducing a scheme of crop insurance whether or not the federal government brought in such a scheme. It cannot be argued that the establishment of a crop insurance scheme in the province of Manitoba has been made possible because of the initiative taken by this government. That, to use the words of the Minister of Agriculture himself, is simply not the case.
It is true that Mr. Willis did say the other day that although he had not seen the bill he was happy that it had been introduced. It cannot be argued from those words that the government of which he is a member was in any way influenced by the initiative of this government. Proposed Crop Insurance
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources gave us the impression that what he wants to do is to woo the farmers of Saskatchewan in particular with less federal support as provided for in this bill than is now provided for under P.F.A.A. Particularly high risk areas present problems beyond the scope of crop insurance as such, and relief for these areas probably requires a separate and distinct government program.

Some failed to give sufficient consideration to excluding submarginal farms and those farms in the areas of highest risk from participation in a crop insurance program.
Why did the minister of northern affairs fail to cite this particular reference? They will be excluded under this bill and they are the people by whom help in this particular is most needed.

Mr. Speaker, we listened with great attention, a lew minutes ago, to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton). He said, among other things, that the Liberals were accusing the government of acting too hastily. I would like him to shed those illusions, for we do not propose to do so. We never accused the government of acting too hastily, but rather of failing to act at all. However, in the present case, we are accusing this government of proceeding somewhat haphazardly.
The minister asked us what was the basis for our criticism of a legislation not yet tried out. On many occasions, during this session, we have realized that the opposition's constructive criticism has made possible certain improvements of the legislation which had been introduced. Moreover, I think it is our responsibility to advance the arguments of those we represent here.
Legislation has now been submitted which tends to establish a crop insurance scheme, and the minister stated that the federal government undertakes to pay 50 per cent of the administration costs, 20 per cent of the amount of premiums asked, and to loan the provinces 75 per cent of the sum required for indemnity exceeding $200,000. Therefore, the provinces will have to bear the burden of 50 per cent of administration costs, or else the farmers bear it.
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who rose in support of his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), dealt only with the problems of the west. I presume that he failed to dwell on the issues facing the eastern provinces because a colleague, that is one of the four ministers from the province of Quebec, might speak on behalf of eastern or Quebec farmers.
As can be seen on page 5230 of the official record of this House of Commons for June 29, 1959, the Minister of Agriculture stated:
As one would expect, the provinces which displayed most interest in it were the three prairie provinces which were all interested in a system of crop insurance and in instituting such a system at the earliest possible time.
We may remember that these provinces have benefited in the past under the P.F.A.A. and that, since 1939, farmers have received, under that legislation, $204 million in the form of deficiency payments half of which had been underwritten by Canadian taxpayers. Therefore, the P.F.A.A. forced all taxpayers to contribute part of the assistance given to the prairie farmers. Now, under this act, which does not apply in a province like

Quebec where mixed farming is practised, taxpayers, as I say, will be called upon to subscribe to legislation that will not solve their problems in any way.
I would not like it to be said that I am taking a negative attitude towards western farmers; rather it should be considered a positive one with regard to eastern farmers, and more particularly those of the province of Quebec.
I was pleased a few moments ago, to hear the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), support the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), especially when he said that this act should apply not only to a single area, but throughout the country. I wonder if this act is viewed with favour in the eastern provinces. We have heard members discussing the matter, and there have been many quotations from western papers, but none from eastern papers, as far as I know. Are we to conclude that this bill is not eliciting as much interest in the eastern parts of the country as was expected by the government? Are we to conclude, having heard only from the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), that other members from the province of Quebec feel that this act would be of very little help, and that it requires our farmers to pay contributions to a plan which cannot settle their problem and will be of no help to them.
The opposition has mentioned repeatedly that this bill on crop insurance should have been referred to a committee. That, it seems to me, would have been the logical procedure in the circumstances, because then the government and the minister would have had the opportunity of consulting farm organizations, such as the U.C.C., the Cooperative Federee, the Interprovincial Farm Union or the National Federation of Agriculture.
The result is that this bill has been introduced without the provinces having been consulted, as the minister himself admits, though the provinces are expected to bear an additional burden. I recall that, just a few weeks ago, while visiting my constituency, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) stated that the present government does not favour centralization and that its aim is to hand back to the provinces the rights to which they are entitled.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a great deal has been said by the minister of northern affairs about the situation in Saskatchewan in so far as this bill is concerned. I do not come from that province and therefore I am not going to discuss the particular matters he raises, but it seems odd to me that he should have been so particularly interested in this bill. It would seem odd also that this bill should have been introduced in the last days of this session when the committees have finished their work and there is no opportunity of examining the bill which, in our opinion, is not nearly as important to the people of the west as the minister of northern affairs seems to think it is. However, I think the bill warranted discussion by the various farm organizations and some consideration by the committee on agriculture.
I believe, too, that although this particular report to which he referred came out of the province of Saskatchewan, and may have been a satisfactory survey of the situation in that province, it does not give the national picture. I believe there are many aspects of crop insurance that are not going to receive consideration. This plan was referred to by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) as a crop insurance program that he could accept. I am not familiar with the farming operations in which the minister is engaged, but I am told that he raises hogs. It may be all very well for him to insure the number of hogs that he has on his farm under this crop insurance plan, but I wonder if the minister is not bringing things down to a level to which they probably should not be brought. This reminds me of that story, which I think we heard once before,

Proposed Crop Insurance concerning the time the minister became interested on a personal basis in the planting of potatoes. This was during the time he was an officer in the army.
It appears that the people in the maritimes know how to plant potatoes and grow them because, in discussing the matter the other day, I was told they never have crop failures in the maritimes. However, I understand when the Minister of Agriculture had something to do with the planting of potatoes he did not allow the boys from Nova Scotia or New Brunswick to plant them because he knew how to plant them, and he planted them so deep they never came up. It would appear to me, therefore, although I am told the maritime potato growers would not apply for this type of insurance because they never have a crop failure, the minister could probably arrange it.
A great deal has been said about this measure following the pattern of unemployment insurance. It has been all very well to tell the farmers of western Canada that the workers have been getting something for nothing for a long time under unemployment insurance, but there are a great many differences between this plan for agriculture and the unemployment insurance plan for workers. Let us examine just what both plans do. In the case of unemployment insurance, the fund was established by the federal government. Each time the federal government added new classes to the unemployment insurance scheme they have always put some money into the fund and not made it necessary for the workers who were unemployed to go to their provincial governments to borrow the money, up to a maximum of 75 per cent, as is the case under the crop insurance scheme. The government put in some money which the workers were going to be able to draw against when the payments established an actuarially sound scheme. If crop insurance were going to be operated in the same manner as unemployment insurance then some money from the treasury would have to be put into the crop insurance scheme.
Second, it would not be a provincial scheme, it would be a federal scheme. It would be a scheme which would apply to everybody who was engaged in the production of the particular crops that were brought under the crop insurance scheme. Unemployment insurance is not a voluntary scheme on a regional basis, it is a compulsory scheme. If you work in a particular industry you are brought under the scheme and so if you were a farmer and grew a particular crop then you would automatically have to belong to that scheme.

This brings us again to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. This is a compulsory insurance scheme affecting one or two particular crops. It has been satisfactory to the west. It is not entirely a subsidy because, as the minister of northern affairs has pointed out, some of the provinces have more or less been able to carry the cost of their own schemes. Between 1939 and 1957 in the province of Manitoba the total paid out to farmers was almost $14 million, and they paid in, with their 1 per cent contribution, $16 million, leaving them a credit in the fund. Saskatchewan, on the other hand, paid out more than the contributions which were received. For the $60 million which the farmers paid in, they received almost $140 million in benefits. Now it would be surprising to me if the people of Saskatchewan were to be very interested in changing the form of compulsory crop insurance they have now for one which does not appear to be as advantageous, one which is obviously going to give them 20 per cent, whereas this plan is giving them more than they have put into the scheme. The province of Alberta has received $50 million and paid in $30 million, so it would seem as if the province of Alberta, also, has been getting an advantage.
The minister may argue that this is one of the reasons why there should be a new scheme. If this is the case, why not extend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act on a national basis and apply it to a number of other crops? It has been argued in this house on innumerable occasions in the past that this could be done with very little difficulty, and probably the premium for Canada would not have to be much higher than it is already. As I said before, producers in the maritimes tell us they never have crop failures. Similarly, in the Niagara area there is very seldom a crop failure in more than one or two commodities, and we must bear in mind the wide range of fruits, vegetables and other products which are grown in this region. In my own area, if we have a very dry year and the hay is not too good, it is very likely we will have a bumper crop of grain, because weather conditions never maintain for such a length of time that we have more than a failure or partial failure of more than one crop in a year; it would be unusual to find so much rain that it would result in a crop failure in coarse grain.
As I say, I think this act could be extended. It is a compulsory act, and one which is already in existence. It is a provision which guarantees to farmers that they will have a sum of money in the event of crop failure, and the provinces do not need to borrow in order to meet their liabilities in the event of such a failure. If we look down

the list and note the demands which have been made under this scheme we will find that there have been some years when the drain has been tremendous. Let us take, for example, the year 1954, and suppose that the scheme now proposed had been in existence. Payments in Manitoba would have amounted to something over $5 million, and in the province of Saskatchewan, to $21 million. In the province of Saskatchewan, in 1953, it was only $1 million as against $21 million in the following year, and in Manitoba it was $5 million in 1954 as compared with only $619,000 in 1953. So that if we had put this scheme into effect in a year in which there was a large number of people taking it and there happened to be a need for crop insurance, then the province, or the municipalities, or whoever were going to pay the 20 per cent, would be in financial difficulties for a number of years to come.
It does not say in this particular bill whether hogs, chickens, specialized game birds or anything else are to be included. I think that depends entirely on what the provincial governments put into their interpretation of the word "crops". This bill says that a crop is an agricultural crop declared to be a crop for the purpose of the act. I assume this would depend on the regulations enacted by the provinces, and I see no reason why the Minister of Agriculture, if he wished, could not guarantee or insure himself against having less than 12 pigs in a litter, or 15. Thus I see that the bill could offer some particular attraction in the hon. gentleman's own area.
These problems could well be discussed. I am not saying that this is not a good thing. I think that if we are going to extend crop insurance it could probably be worked in a way in which we could also have guaranteed production insurance. This would come in very handy at home, where they would like to be able to guarantee five cans of milk where they only have four cans now, or else to guarantee the four that they are getting at present. I am sure my brother would be very happy to participate in a scheme of this type, though I think he would also want it to be extended so as to guarantee the sale of his milk in case everyone else started to produce the guaranteed amount.
In Ontario we have another problem which I think is quite important. We have experienced a great deal of difficulty in the last two years in southern Ontario with regard to fruits and vegetables, and I am sure that hon. members from all parts of the country have received deputations and letters from various producers, particularly tomato producers, cherry producers, peach producers and other fruit growers in the Niagara peninsula. One
Proposed Crop Insurance of the problems that they will have, and which I can foresee, is that if they insure, say, a crop of tomatoes, and the crop has an estimated value of $100 an acre, then I would assume that the farmer would insure it at that value of $100 an acre. If the farmer gets a bumper crop and he has to meet the payment, and if he finds that his cost of production of that acre of tomatoes runs over $50, and the canners are only offering him $20, I fail to see where he is going to get the money to meet his commitment. Obviously, if he had a bad crop he would be in a better financial position because the amount paid to him consequent upon crop failure would presumably be enough to pay the premium. Many of the producers are not able to market their crops when they have a bumper crop and they tell me that sometimes it is more advantageous for them to leave the products on the trees or on the vines than it is to harvest them. So they are going to be hard pressed about coming into any insurance scheme. The minister is looking at this question from the point of view of eventually eliminating P.F.A.A. The present plan would not offer to Ontario with its many diversified crops the type of crop insurance we had been led to believe this government would implement.
What is being offered under this plan has been suggested by a number of provinces. I was told last fall that this type of insurance was going to be introduced in Manitoba whether or not the federal government participated. I assume they are going to pay their percentage of the cost and have already decided what the premium to the producer is going to be. This plan leaves many questions unanswered and many problems farmers will be faced with unsolved.
The honest way for the government to have handled this would have been to introduce the bill and then refer it either at this session or another session to a committee of this house so that farm organizations and commodity groups insuring under the plan could have had an opportunity to make representations. Failing to do this, the minister is only offering window dressing for political reasons.
I think it is safe to say that some of the provinces will take advantage of the bill if only on an experimental basis. Crop insurance should be applicable to everyone in the country. Rates should be low an easily carried by all farmers. Such a scheme could only be introduced following much more extended study than has been given to the matter. This I suggest could only be done if the government allowed the measure to go to a committee so that interested organiza* tions would have an opportunity to make specific recommendations on crop insurance.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should comment briefly on some of the statements and criticisms which have been made today with respect to this bill. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) following the same line did a great deal of talking about more study being required before the scheme is put into effect. As I indicated previously, studies of this subject have been conducted for over 20 years. The result of all that study has not been a single, definite, practical plan of crop insurance being brought forward and proposed by anyone prior to the introduction of the present bill.
What hon. gentlemen opposite are saying in effect is that the matter has been studied but now there should be another year of study; it should not be finished up at this session of parliament; the bill should not go through; there should be at least a further year's study in connection with the matter; we should bring in all the farm organizations and conduct a further extensive study in connection with the matter.
All I can say is that for over 20 years the Liberals delayed in bringing a scheme into operation. Now that we have brought in a farm insurance scheme they want to impose a further year's delay or more as far as passage of the bill is concerned.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River brought up the matter of the United States plan. Without definitely saying so I believe he left the impression that the payments made by the federal government in that country were at least as great if not greater than those proposed in this bill. This is simply not the case as I have already indicated when I spoke at the resolution stage. Under the United States crop insurance plan the administration costs are what the federal government pays and if there is any surplus of premiums over the indemnities paid then some of the premium money can be taken in order to pay the administration costs. That has been done in the past few years. As a matter of fact United States law provides a maximum of $1,500,000 a year which can be taken out of the money paid in as premiums in order to pay administration costs. When the plan was first introduced and they suffered considerable losses some of the original capital of the corporation which was used to administer this was used to pay indemnities. At the present time they are getting a surplus and that has been particularly true during the last few years.


The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River stated that no provision is made in this bill to cover heavy losses if such are experienced under the scheme. As a matter of fact that is what this loan provision is for, so that if heavy losses are experienced in a particular province the financial stability of the province will not be disturbed, due to the fact that we are prepared to loan the province up to 75 per cent of the amount of the losses. That is the whole reason for the loan provision.
The hon. gentleman went on to say that I said that the farm credit bill was one of the most important bills to be introduced in parliament but that I did not say this wih respect to the crop insurance bill. I think it is quite clear that the farm credit bill is a more important bill than the crop insurance one. The farm credit bill goes to the very root of many of our farm problems. It is the type of reform which is necessary if we are to have economic farm units over a large part of this country. Of course, the necessity for improved farm credit exists in every part of the country. The need for farm credit is universal whereas crop insurance needs vary from province to province as I indicated at the resolution stage.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) suggested that the measure should be put over until the next session. I am not surprised at his attitude and in fact I expected him to take that line because he indicated clearly at the resolution stage that he does not really want crop insurance at all. What he wants is a big federal government handout of some kind, but he does not want crop insurance.

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I had been replying to some of the comments and criticisms made by some hon. members opposite in their speeches on second reading of the crop insurance bill. I had practically completed that matter and there is just one other thing about which I think I should say something.
I think the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) indicated either that he had not read the bill or, if he had read it, that he did not understand it because he was talking about insurance for pigs, game cocks and

various other types of livestock. I think it is understood by probably every other member of the house that the crop insurance bill is designed to apply to crops that are grown from the ground. There has never been any intention of insuring livestock, machinery used on the farm or anything else along that line.
The hon. member for Timiskaming says that the bill might be all right for the minister and others who raise hogs, that it might be satisfactory to them to insure their hogs and so on. I want to correct any impression which anyone may have that there was any intention at any time to insure livestock. This is a crop insurance scheme. In other words, it insures crops which grow from the ground -whether it is barley or any other types of crop of that kind-but does not insure what are ordinarily classed together as livestock and chattels.
I think I should at the same time comment on the story which he told in connection with my alleged potato planting activities during the war in England, a story which has been repeated here at least once or twice previously and in very incorrect form. As hon. members know, in 1941, I think it was, there was an army order to all units in England that they were to grow as much of their own food as they could and were to use any land that was not in use for agricultural purposes adjacent to where they were billeted. In pursuance of that order we were given a little bit of heath which happened to be a bit of a dip and therefore was not covered with bushes and so on, and we were told to put in some garden.
I looked it over and decided that perhaps the only thing that could be planted on it was potatoes. Of course the boys in the battery were not very anxious to go to work planting potatoes so they raised all sorts of complaints such as that we had no equipment, no machinery or anything else and that therefore we could not put in this potato crop. I therefore went out to the nearest farm and borrowed a plow, and in planting these potatoes I followed the system which I had seen employed back in 1910 and 1911 by settlers who were coming into western Canada at that time and moving on to homesteads where there was nothing but sod. In other words, it was a matter of plowing a furrow, dropping the potatoes along it and turning the next furrow over them. You do not get a very good potato crop but you get something. We produced quite a few potatoes in spite of the scoffing or the objections, we will say, of some of the men in the battery who were not at all anxious to go into this type of activity.

Clause 4 reads in part as follows:
4. (1) The contribution payable to a province under an agreement shall be paid in respect of each year and shall be the total of
(a)	fifty per cent of the expenses incurred by the province in that year in the administration of the insurance scheme; and
(b)	if the province has by the agreement undertaken to pay a share of the premiums, the lesser of

The minister has said many times that a province will not be required to pay any premiums whatsoever. I think I understand what the clause means but it does require, in the initial stages at any rate, the provinces

Proposed Crop Insurance to pay a share of the premiums. On the surface this provision seems very much at variance with the statement the minister made so many times during the debate, namely that a province would not be required -if it did not wish to do so-to make any contribution towards premiums. Then I should like to know what the length of the period will be from the time the province pays this money into the fund until the federal government reimburses the province.
Would it not be much better and would it not be more accurate in the context of the statement by the minister, to provide that the federal contribution shall be paid directly to the fund and directly to the provincial corporation or agency that is operating the crop insurance and not by this law require the province, at least in the initial stages, to pay a share of the premiums?

The Minister of Agriculture has much greater faith than I in the wisdom of the officials to whom he refers. Yesterday we had not only an instance of the officials in the Department of Justice drafting certain clauses in a bill but of the Minister of Justice himself piloting the measure through the house, and we will all agree that the Minister of Justice is himself a very eminent lawyer. However, you would hardly recognize some of the clauses after parliament itself had improved on what was very slipshod phraseology when the bill was first introduced in the house. All I do at this time on this clause is to protest what the government is doing to the provinces that come under this legislation.
It is recognized by everyone who knows anything about agricultural conditions in Canada that Saskatchewan is not only a major agricultural province but that it is the province of greatest risk. It is the province where there are the greatest number of crop failures. Under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act experience shows that crop failures in Saskatchewan have resulted in payments being made to producers in one

year, namely in 1954, as high as almost $22 million. It is Saskatchewan where the great crop losses can take place.
It is Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan government, the Saskatchewan treasury that the minister is asking by this measure to underwrite the losses. Let no one be misled into thinking that the 20 per cent that the federal government agrees to pay of the premiums means 20 per cent of the losses, because the losses can pile up initially into tremendous losses running into tens of millions of dollars. It will not bankrupt the provincial treasury, initially at any rate, because the federal government will lend the province the money; but it is the province that under this legislation is required to pay and to take up the losses. This legislation is no gift; it is legislation that individuals in high risk areas in Saskatchewan can comply with and can use only at very high cost.
I think the people of Saskatchewan will resent what is in fact discrimination directed against that province because ours is the high risk province, just in the same way as the legislation under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is directed to help in a substantial way the producers in Saskatchewan who are in a high risk area. This also applies, but not to the same degree, of course, to the province of Alberta. This is one of the clauses in this legislation which will be up for public debate. It is one of the clauses which I think is inadequate and that I shall be glad to debate on any occasion with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Minister of Agriculture.
They can dress up this legislation in any way they wish. They can make far-reaching statements that this is going to take care of the incomes of agricultural producers so that they will not have an experience like they had in the thirties, and they can make other statements which mean very little. But the fact is that the people of Saskatchewan, the farmers through individual payments and/or the provincial treasury have to pay a very high cost to use this legislation, and I hesitate not at all in saying that the principles followed in prairie farm assistance have much more to commend them than the inadequate principles in this bill which we hope in the days ahead, after so much criticism on our part, will be improved.

Mr. Chairman, I regard this particular clause as the key and hub of everything we have been talking about, particularly with respect to our expected partners, the provinces. I think that we have to look at this very carefully indeed, and I am quite satisfied that the minister should look again upon his requirement of the provinces with respect to loans advanced by
Proposed Crop Insurance Canada. The minister says in this bill that the loans shall be repayable upon terms that the cabinet at Ottawa unilaterally decides. I do not think that that is going to encourage any provincial government that has any caution at all to go very far toward doing the kind of thing that on all sides of the house we want to see done, namely to establish crop insurance. I think, as I explained earlier, that inasmuch as the federal cabinet is in charge of the actuarial soundness of any scheme in any province they should under those circumstances agree that when loans are made, if the terms of payment of those loans are in accord with what they laid down, they should continue to be the primary lender and retain the primary responsibility. On the contrary, under this bill they can just demand and ask for payment at any time without adequate appreciation of the provincial final liability in this respect.
That I think is of the essence. I do not oppose the thought that it is desirable in a widespread country like ours to have provincial administration in matters of this kind; but, as I said earlier, in every royal commission report that I have looked at the conclusion is that the long term, ultimate liabilities are beyond what a provincial royal commission would advise a provincial government to assume. The commissions say that there is the desirability of having this kind of insurance, but they also say that the diversification must be wider than within one province. However, I find elsewhere in this bill an arbitrary clause which enables the federal government to dictate the terms of these loans, the clause providing the 75-25 per cent proportion. It is not subject to mutual agreement; the loans are settled by the federal organization. I would say that if I were in the provincial sphere I would be very hesitant indeed to undertake the risks which are explained in some of the royal commission reports on crop insurance which I have read.
I think that the minister should look again at this particular clause. I suggest to him that if at the initial stage he and his advisers are in complete charge of determining what is actuarially sound in so far as crop insurance is concerned, it is not right to present a bill and say, "We will loan the provinces 75 per cent of a loss after a bad year", when the provinces have had nothing to do with respect to the assessment of the rates and have not the resources for taking care of emergencies such as many of us remember. Under these circumstances I think that this clause, probably more than anything else in the bill, is likely to be responsible for the failure on the part of sensible provincial

Proposed Crop Insurance administrators to take advantage of this worthy proposal that we should have a national crop insurance scheme.
Mr. Chairman, I am very serious about this. The minister has emphasized the long term aspect. I think he will agree with me that in examining some of the points which have come to light from experience of the only known crop insurance scheme that we have on this continent, namely in the United States, he will find that they have had some difficulty because their rates and their organization are based on too short a term of experience.
The minister seemed to agree with me when he began to talk about the experience from, say 1926 up to the present time, but in western Canada, fortunately, we have very complete and helpful information about crop records in every category going back as far as that date. So if the minister insists that his scheme must be approved by him as actuarially sound, I say that is not much of an encouragement for the provinces. If he then says: I assume no ultimate contingent liability; I only promise after the end of one crop year to lend you 25 per cent of your indemnities that exceed your premiums received beyond $200,000 and so on, I do not think that is consistent. If the minister is in the driver's seat with respect to actuarial soundness I think he must also, if he wants this to be national in scope, stand behind the scheme as an actuarial scheme which he has approved on a long term basis without profit to the producer, since the producer is averaging over a long period of time. But what is proposed in this bill is that the provinces, with slender resources, must undertake repayment of losses which might occur should the federal government's actuarial calculations prove to be wrong, and I think that will deter a great number of the provinces from entering this scheme.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-67, to provide for the extension of long term mortgage credit to farmers.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when this bill was at the resolution stage I indicated most of the main provisions in it, and thus I will not delay discussion of the detailed provisions by further extended remarks at this time.
As was stated then, this bill, along with the amendments to other farm credit legislation, gives a basis for a federal farm credit system which can be developed as a service for the benefit of Canadian agriculture in the years to come. In general, the approach of the government has been to enter the field of farm credit to ensure that family farm operations and those who work their own land or operate their own farms may be able to obtain sufficient credit to cope with what might be termed a rapidly moving commercial agricultural development. In 1921, for example, there were 3,500,000 horses on farms in Canada. Today there are fewer than one million. Their place has been taken, and a great deal more power made available, by tractors. Expenditure on machinery and equipment has greatly expanded all along the line, all of which has required much bigger expenditures as far as farmers are concerned. Livestock operations on farms in Canada have also been increased, with the exception of sheep and lambs. Since the 1920's total farm operating expenses, including depreciation, have about doubled.
It is not possible to refer to Canadian agriculture as other than commercial agriculture. However, there are segments of the agricultural economy where there is a lag in developing economic units. Further, this changeover has meant a greatly reduced labour force in farming, accompanied by a very substantial increase in production per man year. In order that the best personnel, that is those who are likely to continue to increase this production per man year, may be retained on farms, it is the aim of the government to make sure that they have this opportunity in so far as capital required is concerned. This bill makes it possible, through the package deal, for younger, energetic farmers, who may qualify, to make quicker progress in establishment than otherwise might be the case and thus will encourage them to take up farming as their permanent occupation.
5638	HOUSE OF
Proposed Long Term Credit to Farmers
In providing additional farm mortgage credit opportunity there would appear to be little difference between the action proposed in this bill and recommendations made by the two major national agricultural organizations. These organizations have recommended a co-ordinated credit system; they have recommended higher loan values both in dollars and in relation to the equity of the borrower; they have recommended more flexible repayment; they have recommended a system of supervised credit for younger farmers and many other general features, most of which are included within the scope of the proposed farm credit act.
The farm organizations recommended the extension of the total term of loans for a 40-year period from the present 30-year period. As I indicated in the house at the resolution stage, it was felt better to increase the age limit to 45, and that this would give more possibilities of benefit than the extension of the term of the mortgage for an extra 10 years. This is one of the few recommendations of the farm organizations which we have not followed.
While the interprovincial farm union council brief is not specific on interest rate, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture suggests that the government might subsidize the interest rates on loans by the amount of the administration costs. The interprovincial farm union brief in an introductory paragraph states that if the government's attitude toward farm credit would give consideration to the various services that only governments can provide effectively, "most of the farm credit could be provided on as sound and self-supporting a basis as any other commercial credit". Later in their brief they indicate that they wish to have low interest rates for special cases. It may be unfair to suggest that this means that they are asking for subsidized rates.
The government believes, and we hope rightly, that by including the new package deal to provide farmers with the opportunity of operating an economic establishment, this type of farm unit will be able to pay for the full cost of borrowed money. As I stated at the time the resolution was discussed, and I can again assure you, there will be no unnecessary expenditures either for money borrowed or for administration costs.
A calculation by officials of the Veterans Land Act, arising out of a survey which was made among 5,000 veterans on the basis that they would be established on economic farm units, indicates that additional credit would earn 24 per cent after deducting $10 per day


for additional labour. This percentage varied by area and by province but the range was from 12 to 30 per cent.
To a limited extent the government does subsidize the corporation by providing up to $8 million of interest free capital. It has also provided that the reserves of the present Canadian farm loan board will be available to the new corporation without interest cost. Any subsidy beyond this would tend to interfere with provincial and private schemes, including those of a great many co-operatives who are now making agricultural loans.

Just the same people in general are firmly convinced that many farmers were saved from bankruptcy by this legislation. Others have been able to improve their farms which later became economic and self-liquidating units.
In the past, the Canadian farm loan program has always reached the objectives it had set for itself. Whenever changing conditions, farming methods and new needs so

required, the government never delayed in introducing amendments designed to satisfy the agricultural population.
If any criticism can be directed against that measure, it is perhaps for the fact that we have been too prone to provide loans for the betterment of the marginal and even submarginal farm units instead of limiting the loans to farms likely to improve.
These last few years and particularly nowadays, the development of agriculture has changed so much that we will have to change our ideas as far as farm credit is concerned. It will be necessary to provide credit for the very specific purpose of helping the farmer's family to produce more efficiently and profitably in order to secure an income of at least $3,000 for a family of 4 or 5 people.
The new concept that we must have of a modern farm credit system is indicated by the rapid development that we witnessed as a result of new farm production methods and of new market requirements.
For the past 20 years, farm capital has increased by 30 per cent. In the opinion of nearly two thirds of the "Farm Forums" it is necessary today to invest more than $20,000 in order to make a good start in agriculture.
The nature of capital investment also has changed, thus following the general trend.
According to professor William E. Hal-levand, of the department of agricultural economy at Macdonald College, in the province of Quebec, the real estate value, per farm, has increased by 15 per cent, the livestock value by a little more than 30 per cent and the equipment and power value by approximately 94 per cent.
The most noticeable changes have taken place in western Canada as far as equipmenl is concerned, and in eastern Canada as regards livestock improvement.
As a result, it is getting more and more difficult for anyone who wants to engage in agriculture and especially for the young farmer, to settle down on a farm.
Many other reasons would motivate a change. They are:
The decrease in number of capital farms in agriculture. The decrease of cultivated areas particularly in eastern Canada on the fringe of larger cities. The increase of mechanization and the extension of the farming surface. A reduction of farm labour. The growing importance attached to production credit, as compared to land purchase credit.
All those reasons may lead us to foresee the need of more generous funds for each family unit.
The provinces where agriculture is the main industry recognized that need and recently passed a new legislation, or modified existing legislation in this respect.

The report published by the Quebec Farm Loan Board shows that on March 31 last, 56,803 loans totalling $165,991,695 have been granted since the fall of 1936.
That is more loans than were granted by the government of Canada, from 1929 to March 31, 1959. Out of 575,015 farms in operation in Canada in 1956, 54,624 farmers were granted a loan under the federal farm loan act, that is 10 per cent, whereas in the province of Quebec, loans were granted to 56,803 farmers, out of a total of 120,000, i.e., more than 50 per cent. We can tell about the agricultural and political situation of a province when more than 50 per cent of its farmers are indebted to their government, or rather I should say to the Union nationale.

That is how the international council of farming unions came to recommend the establishment of a federal agency under the Department of Agriculture instead of under the Department of Finance. I find that this has been done, and I commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for transferring administration of that agency service to the Department of Agriculture. Such an agency would include a loan supervision service, along the same lines as under the Veterans' Land Act. This suggestion has also been put forward by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which favours a farm credit supervision service. This means that the services of an expert on agricultural matters will be available to borrowers so long as their debt has not been refunded in the proportion of 25 per cent of total assets. Only then will supervision stop.
Both organizations call for a reduction in interest rates. The international congress of agricultural unions suggests that interest should be between 3 and 3i per cent. On the other hand, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture urges that interest rates be equal to government loan costs, plus a fee to provide for a reserve, but suggests that administration be the government's responsibility.
Two other points on which there is general agreement are an increase in maximum amounts to be loaned by the government, and the percentage assessment on property. The maximum amount should be $20,000, and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture recommends an assessment rate of 80 per cent for loans up to $8,000, dropping gradually to 65 per cent for loans between $16,000 and $20,000.
All loans granted based on a 70 to 80 percent assessment should be under the supervision of government experts. Such are the main features of the improvements that should be made to this bill.

speechtext:
We wish to endorse this bill and to give it our support. In doing so we should like to mention not only the good things that are in it but a number of the things which we consider are not satisfactory.
In recent years, in my own area, the old Canadian farm loan board has been reluctant to make loans to farmers. The valuations which they have placed on farm property and the amount they were prepared to lend on cultivated land have been exceedingly low and, in consequence, it was almost impossible for a farmer to borrow sufficient money to enable him to establish himself in the light of present day conditions in agriculture. However, there are, in my opinion complications with regard to extending long term credit, and I think the experience of the work of the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs in relation to the Veterans' Land Act is something which we cannot overlook. Indeed, we should give close consideration to it when we are considering any type of farm credit.
The Veterans' Land Act, in extending credit, made provision for careful supervision, and it seems to me that when we extend long term credit to farmers we could do those farmers no greater disservice than to supply them with a large amount of money, with the consequent necessity of heavy repayments over a long term at considerable rates of interest, unless we supply also a measure of guidance where necessary. It is evident, of course, that the money can only be paid off if the loan which has been advanced is used advantageously. I believe it is generally agreed among farm organizations that farm loans have not served this end. I was surprised to observe the number of loans made to farmers which have been put in the courts for foreclosure during the last few months. In some instances farmers had borowed $2,500 five or six years ago. Their farms are now being foreclosed upon. Although the farmers made some payments and attempted to pay the interest they are still required to pay amounts of over $3,000.
With respect to supervision, I feel it should not be by agreement but by compulsion. No loan should be given to a farmer unless some supervision can be given so that the loan can be repaid on the terms agreed to by the vendor and the borrower and the farmer can maintain his standard of living on the farm when making these payments. It would not be advantageous for a farmer to obtain a loan that would not directly increase his
