Proposed Long Term Credit to Farmers productivity so that his income would be increased by an amount that would make it possible to repay the loan and maintain if not increase his standard of living.
Several other things should be in the bill. One is the provision of a definite interest rate. Interest rates in Canada have been rapidly increasing. Because of government policy we are now in the position where the government pays interest rates of 5i per cent on one year borrowings. The interest rate should be set at a reasonable level of 5 per cent or less to be of assistance to the farmer. We should bear in mind the experience we have had under the Veterans' Land Act. If it is left open as it appears to be in the bill it will be found that interest rates of 6 to 61 per cent on long term borrowings will obtain and these will not be advantageous to the farmer. A farmer would consider himself well off if he were to make a 5 per cent profit on his investment of $30,000 or $40,000.
There is one other major defect in this bill and I refer to insurance. We have just discussed the crop insurance bill which took into consideration crop failures. We must include a clause to make it possible for a mortgagor in borrowing money from the federal government not to have to make any payment on the principal of his loan if the area-not just his farm but the area in which he lives-is declared to be a disaster area or a depressed area or one where the crop fell below a certain percentage. This would not be expensive insurance. There have been requests from many sources for consideration of a similar provision with respect to mortgages on houses. It has been requested that when an area is in a depressed state because of unemployment the people holding mortgages should be exempted from payments on principal. This could also apply to credit for farmers.
Once a farmer falls behind in his payments and the interest begins to compound it is almost impossible for him to catch up on his double payments regardless of how well' he may do next year.
We should also extend sickness insurance to this bill. Few farmers are covered by sickness and accident insurance. When a farmer falls ill and cannot do his work the mortgage payments build up. I know of a case where a farmer took ill for two years. The farm ran down during that period and his payments had not been made. Pressure was being exerted on him by the machinery companies and by the Canadian farm loan board. One would not expect the board to have pressed him. When he was finally able to work he reached the conclusion that he could not recoup his losses and so the farm


was sold. He simply could not see his way clear to ever catching up on the payments.
If the government can give no consideration to mortgage insurance for sickness and crop failure I urge it to give consideration to assisting the farmer to carry on under a life insurance policy to cover the full extent of the loan, even if this is done at the expense of the mortgagor. This should not be a surprising suggestion and it would not be an expensive type of insurance. If I go to Household Finance Company to borrow money to buy an automobile the company will insure the loan. If I die owing the money even the Household Finance Company with all its faults will arrange it so that the family can own the automobile and not have to make payments on it. I see no reason why this government cannot at least put into the legislation a compulsory feature of having life insurance on the mortgagor so that when the breadwinner of the family dies the mortgage is covered.
This matter is very important Mr. Speaker, because there are hundreds of thousands of farmers in Canada who have had mortgages on their farms all their lives and when they die they will be leaving their families with mortgages that they have been struggling all their lives to pay off. I think we can do no less than assure that when they die, if at no other time, they will leave to their families farms without mortgages.

Mr. Speaker, I realize this is a very improper time to rise but I assure the house that I will not impose upon them. I want to be called if I am longer than about two minutes. This subject is something that I spoke about when the Veterans' Land Act amendments were up. Afterwards, I heard from indirect sources that I had spoken rather wildly when I suggested that the same volume of loans outstanding under the Veterans' Land Act could be taken care of by the same civil service staff as is contemplated would be required by the new program. I just want to give one or two instances to the house. The Veterans' Land Act had 3,000-plus fewer borrowers last year than the year before. They added only 260. Everybody can appreciate that they need a fairly constant staff in the supervisory work that we know they do very well.
The minister has introduced a new feature,, in connection with general farm loans, of a supervisory character. I notice that the bill contains a reference to the utilization of the Veterans' Land Act people, but I hope it is not just a form that is put in there, because I am satisfied that while the Veterans' Land Act loans outstanding at the moment come

to about $200 million, because of our widespread geography they are, shall we say, under-employed, and I am satisfied that they could take on within a year or two at least an extra amount of new borrowings of $100 million and give the appraisal, the inspection, the counsel and the advice needed. I hope the minister will assure us that co-operation will exist.
In January we were told that we would have a centralized farm credit organization. That, apparently, has not developed but I hope the minister will assure us later that we are not going to have another empire set-up under his department in connection with part III of this bill.
I want to commend the minister on the basic terms of this new legislation. I think they are very appropriate. On the other hand, we must remember that even under the former regime, from 1952 to 1956, the maximum amount of loans went up from $5 000 to $15,000 and the maximum appraisal value went up from 50 per cent to 65 per cent.
In so far as the interest rate is concerned, I agree with the last speaker that it is not very conclusive in the bill as to what the interest rate will be, although the minister indicated this was going to be a self-supporting scheme, as the Canadian farm loan scheme has been in the past. It is to the credit of the former scheme that it has never incurred a loss to the taxpayers of this country. In the banking and commerce committee last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) paid tribute to that. He indicated that a reduction in interest rates of even one per cent would put the Canadian farm loan board into a deficit position. The profit they showed last year was equivalent to a reduction in the interest rate of only one-tenth of 1 per cent. I objected last year, not to the stabilization of the interest rate under the direction of the Minister of Finance; I simply said it was in contravention of the statutes passed by parliament. I understand that under the new bill the board again is the organization that
